entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour, from its own timer, on the checklist the owner supplied, starting from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour, from its own timer, on the checklist the owner supplied, starting from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in "Hourly reviews, 11 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:05The best hour of verified code at thirty lanes, a repair of 488 published files measured, and a pipeline the coordinator broke with that repair and wrongly reported as passing. Between 23:02 and 00:04: verified code up by 20,556 bytes in 248 functions (19,893 bytes an hour, against 14,141 over the last 24 hours); 42 routines lifted, to 1,311. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 265 functions and 20,340 bytes in 30 lane-hours, with six claims held. Nothing was withdrawn. 488 published files that did not build alone were replaced by repaired files, each built alone and run against its proving lane's contract of record first; the assembled library then took 19,414 of 19,632 verified rewrites and left out 218, where it had left out 706. Lifting moved from leaf functions to classes: the seek-cover tasks (11 methods), the motion tree's composer (18) and a spatial-library class (4) are in, each with unsafe code forbidden in its module, and the audio engine's base sound class (9) is tested and waits for a green pipeline. The class lanes read verified rewrites more closely than anything before them and found, in one evening: three header comments that contradict their code, a contract that draws five routes on which the original faults, a contract that covers four of eight child slots, and two more contracts with a zero stack fill hiding an uninitialised read. Two partly proven functions of one to two kilobytes were verified whole by Haiku lanes, each on the first attempt under the new brief, with four and seven wrong versions rejected; three others gained four to thirteen proven stages and stay open. The stack-fill audit stands at 136 settled of 2,081: 106 depend on the zero fill, 29 pass with the pattern as well.The coordinator's faults this hour, in order of weight. It told the owner that the pipeline run measuring the repair had passed; it had read that run's manifest and not its conclusion. The assembled-library job passed and the lift-test job failed, because one older lift test crate supplied a constant that a repaired rewrite now defines for itself. Three lift commits were pushed onto the failing pipeline before the scorecard showed it. The statement is corrected in chat and in the changelog; the crate is fixed after building all 80 lift test crates to find every such collision (it was the only one); the run on the fix is queued, and no tracked code is committed until its conclusion, read as a conclusion, is success. The repair commit also took two commits where one was meant, from a list of paths that assumed one folder. The rule that would have prevented the main fault is now applied: before a change to verified files is committed, every crate that includes verified files is built. On proofs: the coordinator's re-run at 300 trials has now twice held a good claim whose wrong version fails on under one trial in a hundred; held claims of that kind are re-run at the contract's own count before they are treated as holds, and five more are being re-run so now. The three blockers. First, the coordinator's rate of error under its own rate of change, now seven slips in three hours and one of them a false report: fewer changes per hour, each validated before the next, is the correction, and the lanes do not need the coordinator to move this fast. Second, proofs that cover less than they say, where the class lifts have become a second, independent audit. Third, the owner's open decisions: the lane count, and the host-platform experiment. Accelerating against the 24-hour baseline.

How to reproduce it

The scorecard is printed by the review script in the coordinator's folder from the verified index, the lanes' results and logs, the changelog and the machine's own counters; each row's figures are that script's output at the time given.

entry.title: Shaft channel steps (spdShaft) lifted from their verified rewrites and proven
entry.summary: From lane l-cls17.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls17.

What was asked

Lift the shaft class of the engine's spatial library, the family named by the executable's type information, from its verified 32-bit rewrites to portable Rust that owns its data. Lift only what is verified, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite.

What the family is

The class has four step methods, all verified: each advances one of four channels by a step length and returns the channel's third direction seed. Each step stores the length, works out three direction seeds from one gain, one of two calibration pairs and a table of twelve floats, mixes the seeds with the table, and clears a pending byte. The seeds are normalised unless a flag byte is set, in which case each channel uses a fixed unit axis. The constructor and the matrix update are unverified and are not lifted. The physical meaning of the step is not established (Unknown).

FactValueStatus
Verified step methods4 of 6 listed methodsVerified: rewrites and their checker contracts
Lifted and proven4 of 4Verified: differential test on the 32-bit target
Steps compared bit for bit160,101 over 20,000 objectsVerified: test run
Deliberate faults caught5 faults, each on all 4 channelsVerified: test run
Unsafe code in the lifted module0 (the rewrites had 52 tokens)Verified: count

What was found

The header comments of the verified rewrites for three of the four channels give the fixed seeds when the flag is set as the unit vector on the first axis. The code, which the checker's contracts compare with the original, uses a different axis for each channel. The contracts exercise that path, so the comments are the error. Verified by reading the rewrites and their contracts.

The square-root helper that every step calls is a callee outside the game-function database. A port must supply a root that matches the original's helper bit for bit. Whether the helper is correctly rounded is not established.

Two of the first mutants were equivalent: swapping the operands of the cross-seed product changes no result, because the two operands carry the same not-a-number. A table product swap is observable, and a probe confirmed that a not-a-number takes its payload from the first operand under this build's code generation.

What was decided

The lifted methods take a host trait for the square-root callee and return the third seed. Each product and sum pins its operand order with a value barrier. Wrong versions are a second writing of the steps with one deliberate fault each, run on every channel; a control writing with no fault must agree with the rewrites before the faults count.

How to reproduce

Run the host tests of the shaft module in the maths crate, then the differential test crate on the 32-bit target with a time limit. The test crate includes the tracked rewrite files by path and needs the game's constants read from the executable's mapped image.

entry.title: Lifting the motion composer: combining filter, data block and sequencing methods
entry.summary: From lane l-cls14.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls14.

What was asked: turn the verified 32-bit rewrites of three classes of the motion tree's optimised composer into portable Rust that owns its data, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite. What is reported: 18 of the 31 verified methods lifted and proven; 13 deferred with reasons; 23 unverified methods of the same classes not touched.

What the family looks like

The combining filter is a poll tree: a child list, one mode word that marks each child as an OR-term or an AND-term, and a fold accumulator that shares the mode word. The optimised data block holds two bulk tables, cleared and rebuilt as a unit. The composer's own methods sequence work: most of them first run the composer's pending-list drain through its own virtual slot, unless immediate mode is on, then step a sequence counter or forward to one numbered callee. The composer's slots for the drain, the gate pass and the node handler are themselves verified methods, so a composition can bind them to the lifted code.

What was lifted and how it is proven

Each class is one owning type. Every call the original makes to code that is not lifted is a method of a trait, so the proof compares every call in order with its arguments, along with the results and every word the rewrite writes. Each proof runs on real 32-bit objects through the shared checker runtime; the tests are seeded and run in under a fifth of a second. Each lifted method has a deliberately wrong copy in the same run, and each is caught. Twenty-seven differential tests and thirty host edge tests pass.

What the proofs found

A rewrite's doc comment gives the wrong return value for the table reset: the code returns a different offset than the comment states. The lift follows the code, which the run confirms, and the comment should be corrected. The poll rewrite reads eight inline child slots, but the checker's contract draws child counts only from zero to four and the negative values, so counts five to eight agree with the rewrite and are not verified against the original.

What is still missing

Thirteen verified methods are not lifted. One returns an address computed from the inner block, and the record family (twelve methods) stores per-opcode node records with payloads taken from argument memory, handler calls through pointers read from that memory, and address arithmetic on arguments. Those need a decision on opaque derived handles and a node-record model per opcode. The four callees of the forwarders and the drain are unverified methods of the same class and need lifting before those forwards can run in a port. Thread-local lookups for the filter owner and the block manager belong behind a thread-context trait in the platform crate.

entry.title: Seek-cover task family lifted: eleven of twelve verified methods proven
entry.summary: From lane l-cls15.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls15.

Asked. Lift the two pedestrian cover-seeking task classes, the plain seek-cover task and its shooting variant, from their verified 32-bit rewrites into portable Rust, with a differential proof for each method and a deliberately wrong lift of each that the proof must catch.

Found (Verified). The family has fifteen listed methods: twelve verified and three unverified. Eleven of the twelve verified methods are lifted. Each lifted method runs against its rewrite on 1500 generated trials on the 32-bit target. The comparison covers the return value, every callee call in order with its arguments, a copy of the object at each call, and the bytes written. All eleven proofs agree, and all eleven wrong versions are caught. The host tests (25) pass on the 64-bit host.

ClassMethods lifted and provenNot lifted
Seek-cover taskFull, cover-row and short constructors; destructor; subtask router; node allocator (6 of 6)None
Shooting variantScalar deleting destructor; pursuit action; firing-node builder; subject initialiser; type-tag chain check (5 of 6)The think tick (verified, large); three unverified methods

Limits (Verified). The lifted code has no unsafe blocks and no addresses. Every collaborator, including the task pool, the cover table, the virtual slots and the subject, is a method of a trait the caller supplies. The family makes no operating-system calls. Null collaborators, which fault in the original, return early in the port; the proofs do not draw them.

Inferred, to check. The verified router's contract pins flag words whose low bits select a route that the rewrite's own comment describes as faulting in the original. Trials on those routes may prove nothing. Routes zero to two are unaffected.

Left open. The think tick is the largest verified method of the family (about 2000 bytes, about thirty-seven callees, scripted output buffers, float gates and four objects). It needs a memory model for several objects and was not attempted to a sound standard in this lane. Its three unverified neighbours are not lifted.

Decided. Virtual-slot meanings are taken from how the verified rewrites use them, not from the class's vtable, and are marked as such in the registry. The callee names in the rewrites' evidence are proposals and were not adopted.

entry.title: Harvest of 1977 small verified functions: 44 instances proven against six existing routines
entry.summary: From lane l-free28.
entry.content:
From lane l-free28.

What was asked. Take the 1977 small verified functions that call nothing and have no portable counterpart yet, match each against the lifted routines that already exist, and prove every match against its verified 32-bit rewrite. No new lifted routine was to be written in this lane.

What was found.

Routine (existing)Instances provenResult
constant writes (object)261,000 cases each; wrong versions caught
constant writes (global region)3same
field store1same
field pair store3same
row address1same
ratio cell (vehicles)10same

Only 44 of the 1977 functions match. Most are branched, loop over memory, or read through pointer forms the extractor does not take. Of the 143 straight-line functions, 129 groups share an effect shape (order of stores and loads, widths, value kinds), and the largest group has five members. The existing routines are narrower than these shapes: they take a single width, or constants only, or two word parameters. Those groups are the candidates for a later lift.

What was decided. A match counts only if its rewrite compiles from the repository and its test passes on the 32-bit target. Three rewrites call helpers or a runtime name that no tracked file defines; they are listed and not worked around. Two matches were dropped from the global-region crate: one spans about six mebibytes of globals, which the test region cannot hold, and one has named-constant operands its matcher placed wrongly.

Matcher findings. The shipped extractor for the earlier lane accepts an indexed read whose return is a comparison, and accepts a function that stores through a pointer it cannot parse. The proof of the first failed and was caught by the test. The second was guarded out. The rewrites were not wrong in either case. The matcher's return rule and store count should be checked before its matches are reused.

Test runtime. The global-region runtime is a byte array, so a four-byte access at an instance's own address can be unaligned in the test. Rust's debug alignment check aborts on it. The lane's test profile turns debug assertions off; x86 allows the access, and the comparison is unchanged.

How to reproduce. The matcher is the earlier lane's extractor, run over the harvest list with two extra access forms and two guards (a store count and a return-operator check). The families come from the same extractor, grouped by effect shape with offsets and constants removed. The test crates are generated from the earlier lane's generators with this lane's names.

11 October 2026

entry.title: Counted-run search, table reset, flagged stores and record access: 35 instances proven in seven families
entry.summary: From lane l-free27.
entry.content:
From lane l-free27.

Asked. Lift a group of 154 verified small functions that call nothing (27 of 38 bytes, 28 of 39, 24 of 40, 27 of 41, 28 of 42, 20 of 43; 6,221 bytes), by finding the families they belong to and lifting each family once.

Found. The names did not decide the families; the rewrites did. Grouping by what each rewrite reads, writes, returns and branches on gave seven families of four or more members, two of them instances of routines that are already lifted. Most of the rest are singletons or groups of two or three. Five of the 154 cannot be checked, because their rewrites call helpers that no tracked file defines or have no export.

FamilyMembersWhat the routine doesWhere it lives
Counted-run search8Compares a word with each entry of a counted run inside an object, in order, and answers a flag, an index, a masked address or a masked keyNew lifted module counted_run
Sentinel table reset4Clears 128 eight-byte records to an empty marker and a zero half-word, clears an optional flag byte before the run, and returns the endNew lifted module sentinel_table
Flagged pair store4Writes two parameters into two fields of an object, sets or ORs a flag byte between them, and returns a fixed valueNew lifted module flagged_pair_store
Record word read5Reads a record pointer and a validity byte from global tables by index, answers a fixed value for the null index and for a missing record, and otherwise reads one word of the recordNew lifted module record_word_read
Guarded record store and flag read4Stores a byte, a word or a scaled word into a record selected by index, guarded by its validity byte or its pointer; reads one flag byte of a recordNew lifted module record_field_access
Constant initialisers6Writes constants, and the address of a class vtable word, into fixed fields and returns the objectExisting constant_writes, unchanged
Block copies4Copies four words between the object and one caller buffer, in one directionExisting word_block, unchanged

Verified. Each instance was run against its verified rewrite on the 32-bit target with 1,000 generated cases: the returned value and every byte of the memory the rewrite can touch were compared. No instance differed. Every deliberately wrong version of every family (a wrong offset, a wrong stride or count, a wrong constant, a wrong answer form or null answer, a missing or extra store, a flipped guard, a wrong return) was caught on every instance: 123 wrong-version runs in all. The host edge tests pass on the 64-bit host, and the workspace check passes there too.

Decided. Families under four members are listed and left, as the brief says. The streaming record accessors share one global table and one null index: nine routines in all. They split by shape into a read family of five and a store family of four, and both are proven here. The float clamp-and-store routines (three members, one global maximum), the slot-state byte tests (three), and the bit-field readers (three) are listed with their shapes.

Process finding. A wrong version that differs only at one fixed position of a run is caught only when the generated inputs place the single equal word there. The first run of the search family missed a run shifted by one word on one instance, with 1,000 cases and random words. Generating one case in four with exactly one equal entry, at the first, the last or a random place, made every wrong version caught.

Process finding. A wrong version that changes a guard can write through a pointer the original never writes through. The generated states must follow the original's guard, not the wrong version under test, or the rewrite itself faults on the test's memory. Separately, a rewrite that calls a helper no tracked file defines is not counted: three word-copy routines of the audio meters use such helpers and are listed as missing.

Process finding. An instance of a family that is already lifted is the cheapest proof: the existing routine is unchanged and only the instance table and a test crate are new. Two of the seven families were proven this way (constant initialisers, word-block copies).

entry.title: Three small verified families lifted to Rust, and two existing routines proven on four more rewrites
entry.summary: From lane l-free26.
entry.content:
From lane l-free26.

Asked. Lift a group of 168 verified functions of 26 to 36 bytes that call nothing, by finding the structure they share, and prove each lifted routine against its verified rewrites.

Found. The group is not mostly one routine. A hash of normalised bodies splits it into 157 groups; a skeleton of the operations (reads, writes, branches and returns, with widths, offsets and constants removed) gives 152. Three families of four members are real, and two existing lifted routines match four more rewrites. The remaining 152 functions are families of two or three, or odd members, and are listed, not lifted.

FactValueMeaning
Functions on the list168 (5255 bytes)Verified rewrites of small functions that call nothing
Proven instances16 (465 bytes)Three new families of four, one existing routine on three instances, one existing routine on one instance
Lifted routines added3Each is a small parameter row with one method, in its own module; no address, no unsafe code, no pointer-width dependence
Proof16 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery word the rewrite writes compared, and every returned value where the rewrite returns one
Wrong versions4 or 5 per familyEach caught by every instance of its family
Teeth checks3A deliberately altered lifted routine fails the differential test on its first case in every family
Listed, not lifted152 functionsFamilies of two or three (listed by name) and odd members

Verified. The five test programs pass on the 32-bit target (two tests each), and the lifted modules' host unit tests pass (120). cargo check --all-targets exits 0 for the lane's crates on the 64-bit host.

Decided. The three new routines are weak lifts: each is one conditional, table or byte store over a table of instances, and they are reported as such. Their narrowing is recorded in the lane's results: the table lift panics past the end of the table, where the original reads without a check; the float lift passes the value as bits and compares by IEEE value, so a not-a-number is always written and positive and negative zero are equal.

Process finding. Role extraction, not text hashing, is what finds the families. A hash split the largest family across many groups; the skeleton grouped it. A family's parameters should still be read by a script with a shape check, never transcribed by hand.

Unverified. The symbol names of two members of the three-byte family carry a big-endian hint, while the verified rewrites store the least significant byte at the lowest offset. The lift follows the rewrites. The names should be checked against the original before a port uses them.

Still open. Per-module matchers for most existing routines have not been written; a skeleton scan found no further matches. The 152 listed functions are not lifted.

entry.title: Lift of small free functions by shape: 12 families, 79 instances proven
entry.summary: From lane l-free24.
entry.content:
From lane l-free24.

11 October 2026

What was asked. Lift the 211 verified small free functions that call nothing (sizes 12 to 23 bytes) to portable Rust, by finding the routines they are instances of, proving each lifted routine against the verified 32-bit rewrite of every instance, and reporting what is left.

What was found. Role extraction, not names, groups the rewrites: each rewrite's pointer accesses, constants, lets and return were read by a script, and each family matched by shape. Matching the shapes of the listed rewrites gives 79 instance proofs over 78 distinct rewrites, in 12 families. Four families reuse lifted routines already in the repository without change (constant writes, field stores, indexed reads, word tests). Two more reuse existing routines over a region of globals (the constant fill, and the constant writes). Six families are new: a byte flag test, a field-pair store, a packed low-byte flag, a field-to-slot copy, a field comparison, and a row address.

FamilyInstancesLifted routine
Constant writes into an object18existing
Field store of one parameter10existing
Indexed read of a table in an object6existing
Word test (equal, not equal, signed greater)9existing
Fill of consecutive global words6existing constant fill
Constant writes into globals3existing constant writes
Byte flag test (one byte, one mask)4new
Field-pair store5new
Packed low-byte flag5new
Field copied to a global slot4new
Field comparison with a constant5new
Row address of a table4new

What was decided. Each family is one routine on a small data type, with the instance table generated from the rewrite text. Every instance runs 1,000 generated cases against its rewrite, and three deliberately wrong versions per family must each be caught by every instance. The global families run against a test region that the rewrites' global addresses are mapped into; the row family resolves its base the way the rewrite does, and the lifted routine takes the resolved base. The new modules contain no unsafe code. Several lifts are weak: the fill, slot-copy, field-store and row-address families each reduce to one assignment or one arithmetic expression over a table of instances.

What was found that needs review. Nine listed rewrites cannot compile from the repository: six reference constants that no tracked file defines, one calls a helper its file does not define, and two call a helper that only the test crate would provide. They are listed, not worked around. The six with undefined constants are marked verified in the index, so their status should be checked by the checker's owner.

Reproduce. Run the role extraction over the listed rewrites, generate the test crates, and run cargo test -p for each crate with the 32-bit target. The host check of the scratch workspace has no errors and no warnings.

entry.title: Static-row, constant-write and cookie-seal families: 36 instances proven, two new lifted methods
entry.summary: From lane l-free25.
entry.content:
From lane l-free25.

Asked. Lift a group of 141 verified call-free functions of four small sizes, by finding the data structure they share and lifting each routine once, and prove every instance against its verified rewrite.

Found. The group is not one class. Three families account for 36 members. Twenty-six routines write a four-word block in the image's data: a relocated constant, two zeros, and a second relocated constant, returning zero or nothing. Six routines write constants at fixed offsets into their object and return zero, one or the object's address; the existing constant-write lift already has this shape. Four routines stamp an object with a cookie derived from a global counter. The other 105 members are in groups of at most four that differ in shape on reading, or are single.

FactValueMeaning
Static-row members26Two source forms of one four-word write: four 32-bit stores, or two 64-bit stores of the same words
Constant-write members6Constant stores into an object, returning zero, one or the object's address; proven against the existing lifted routine
Cookie-seal members4The four bodies differ only in the vtable constant and the width of one store; after normalising those two places they are identical
Lifted code addedtwo modulesA row writer and a cookie seal, with no unsafe code and no addresses
Proof36 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery word of the table, or every byte of the object, and the counter where the routine has one, are compared
Wrong versionsthree to four per instanceA changed constant, a store left out, a zero word written as one, a shifted offset, a changed return, a counter not advanced; each caught by every instance

Verified. The three test crates pass on the 32-bit target: 26 row instances, 6 constant-write instances and 4 cookie instances, none failing. The host check of the whole lane tree passes, and the lifted modules' host tests pass.

Decided. The row family is lifted as a small parameter type with one method. It is a weak lift: four stores of two constants and zeros. It is counted as such. The cookie seal is a real lift: it mixes an old word with a counter under a mask, advances the counter, and stores in the original's order. The constant-write family is proven against the existing method without changing it.

Process finding. The first grouping by a hash of the normalised text split one routine into many groups, because the same routine appears in two source styles. Grouping by role, from a script that extracts each function's writes, reads, branches and return, and asserts the shape of every member, put the members together. A member that fails the assertion is listed with its reason and left out.

Process finding. The 64-bit stores of one row form are not 8-byte aligned in some members. A debug build's alignment check aborts on them, so that test crate switches the check off, as an existing crate does for the same reason.

Still open. One member of the band reads a word of an uninitialised local array and stores it into the table; it is listed, and its contract should be checked. The 105 other functions have no family of four members of one shape, and are listed.

entry.title: Sixteen verified rewrites withdrawn in a day and all sixteen proven again: what the causes were, and what a proof with ordinary inputs cannot see
entry.summary: This closes the account opened in the entry "Widening a proof's inputs" earlier today, which stood at seven. Over the day sixteen rewrites that had passed their proofs were shown to differ from the original, were withdrawn, had their causes located, and were proven again on contracts that would have caught the fault. Not one of the sixteen was caught by its contract of record: in every case where it was tried, the contract of record passes the faulty form as well.
entry.content:
This closes the account opened in the entry "Widening a proof's inputs" earlier today, which stood at seven. Over the day sixteen rewrites that had passed their proofs were shown to differ from the original, were withdrawn, had their causes located, and were proven again on contracts that would have caught the fault. Not one of the sixteen was caught by its contract of record: in every case where it was tried, the contract of record passes the faulty form as well.

What was asked

If a proof is a thousand random trials inside the ranges its contract declares, what kinds of fault survive it, how are they found, and what does it take to prove the corrected form properly?

The causes

CauseRewritesWhy ordinary trials passed
A float converted to an integer with a cast, where the original's instruction gives a fixed result for not-a-number and for values that do not fitEight, as the first or a later faultContracts draw small floats. The two forms agree everywhere but at the ends of the range and for not-a-number.
A float comparison written with the neighbouring predicate: "not less than" for the original's "not less than or equal"FourThe two differ only when the operands are equal, and random floats are never equal. In one of the four the code was also unreachable under its contract.
An integer comparison with the wrong signednessTwoThe values drawn never had the top bit set.
A read taken from the wrong place on the stack: the neighbouring frame slot, two slots merged into one, a key read from the caller's row where the original reloads the table'sTwoThe contract filled the two places with the same value, or with zero.
A read made earlier than the original makes it, or once where the original repeats itOne, twice overNo trial put a null where the early read would fault, and no callee changed the table between the repeated reads.
Two arguments of a call in the wrong orderOneThe contract's inputs made the two interchangeable.
A float sum whose operand order was not pinnedOneThe order shows only in the payload of the result when both operands are not-a-number.
Logic: an early return that skips a final check, a missing test of a flag bit, a missing branch, AND where the original has OR, an index that the original wrapsFour, with five such faults between them, each behind another faultThe inputs never took the path: an empty range with a negative limit, a flag bit never set, an index never negative.
A constant written into the rewrite where the original loads it from the imageOneThe contract never varied the image's value.

The counts add to more than sixteen because most rewrites had more than one fault. At least eight of the sixteen showed a second, third or fourth fault only after the first was corrected and every input was widened; one had four that all had to be corrected before any widened run passed.

What was learned about proofs

  • A proof covers the inputs its contract draws and the memory its contract compares, and nothing else. Three further gaps of that kind were measured the same day, apart from input ranges: 54 contracts of record set a value at an address inside the code section, where the function never reads it; 148 leave a write to data uncompared; 2,081 set the stack fill to zero, and in a sample of forty about one in six of those proofs depends on the zero in what the function stores.
  • Reading is not enough to withdraw, and not enough to clear. An audit read the original's instruction behind three float comparisons and found the predicate wrong in each. One was then shown on the checker and withdrawn; one was shown once its contract's addresses were corrected; the third has the wrong predicate and no observable difference, because what the comparison selects is added to a zero, and it stayed verified. Nothing was withdrawn on a reading alone, and for one of the three that restraint was right.
  • A widened contract can itself be wrong. Two rewrites that failed widened contracts were cleared: in one the contract widened a word in memory without the scripted callee answer that holds the same word, and in the other the only failing trials were ones on which the original itself faults.
  • Three functions read a frame word they never wrote. For two the proof now holds only for a zero in that word and says so as its first narrowing; for the third the original turned out to overwrite the word before any read, which the lane established from the instructions.
  • The method that located the hardest case, four faults in one function's use of its stack, was a map: every access through the stack pointer resolved to its real frame slot, accounting for pushes and for callees that clean their own arguments, set side by side with the rewrite's variables. The script takes any function.

What was decided

  • Withdraw on a difference shown on the stock checker on trials the original completes, the same hour; prove again only with every input the function reads widened, the special values counted on completed trials with an instrumented copy, and the withdrawn form run as a wrong version that must fail.
  • The production brief carries the rules as versions b27 and b28: predicates and signedness from the original's instruction, arguments against the pushes, operand order pinned, memory read where and as often as the original reads it, values loaded from the image, addresses checked against the function's own operands, no zero stack fill to make a proof pass, and what a contract must reach to see each.
  • The checker's driver refuses a contract that sets a value in code. The audits of the three measured gaps continue as unattended runs; each ends in a list to withdraw and a list of contracts to strengthen.

How to reproduce it

Each rewrite's strengthening lane left, beside its corrected rewrite: the contract of record, the widened contract, a contract per wrong version identical to its partner but for the library, the verdicts, and the counts of special values that reached the corrected code on completed trials. The coordinator ran each set again on the stock checker before importing it. The changelog entries titled "Rewrites: … withdrawn" give each withdrawal's evidence, and the entries "… more functions pass the checker" that follow them give the re-imports.

entry.title: Seven small free-function families lifted: 58 instances proven against their verified rewrites
entry.summary: From lane l-free23.
entry.content:
From lane l-free23.

Asked. Lift the 186 verified call-free functions of a few small sizes by finding the routines they share, lifting each once, and proving every instance against its rewrite.

Found. A text hash leaves 174 of the 186 in singleton groups, because the rewrites are written in many forms. Masking every number and renaming identifiers gives a usable grouping for the larger families, and reading what each rewrite does settles the rest. Seven families were lifted: 10 row lookups, 22 three- and four-word block copies, 8 one-source three-target fan-outs, 4 slot-record stores, 4 task-id flag bits, 4 constant fills and 6 field predicates. Each family is one routine on a small owning type, and a table of instances holds the constants.

FactValueMeaning
Instances proven58Verified rewrites whose lifted routine agrees with them on 1,000 generated cases each, with a wrong version of the routine caught for each
Weak lifts34Block copies (22), fan-outs (8) and constant fills (4): each is one data movement with a return rule
Unsafe in lifted code0The rewrites they replace hold 107 uses of unsafe across 50 files
Not reached128Families below four members, singletons and routines not reduced to a shared shape

Decided. The lifted routines live in new modules of the core crate, one line each in its module list, and nothing else in the crate changes. Each family's test crate includes the tracked rewrite files by path and runs the lifted routine against them on the 32-bit target. The host build of each test crate checks, and the lifted modules carry their own unit tests on the 64-bit host. None of the lifted routines computes with a float. Two broadcast rewrites copy a float through a single-precision load and store; the lift copies the bits, and the test compares them bit for bit on generated patterns, including not-a-number patterns, and they agree. The float helpers that four copy rewrites declare are never called on their path.

How to reproduce. Group the verified rewrites with the number-masked form, then read the role of each rewrite; the family tables and their parameters are in the lane's generator scripts. Build a test crate with the 32-bit target and run it. The differential harness runs each instance on a fresh generated state, compares every word the rewrite may write, and checks that the rewrite's result matches the lifted result.

Confidence. Verified for the seven families on this lane's runs. Inferred for the claim that the families cover the shapes in the group: the 130 others were not checked one by one against a shared shape. The parameters of the block-copy family were transcribed by reading each rewrite; the tests would show a wrong transcription, and none was found.

entry.title: Small free functions: 83 instances in five families proven against lifted routines
entry.summary: From lane l-free22.
entry.content:
From lane l-free22.

Asked. Lift a group of 155 verified free functions of 13, 15 and 17 bytes that call nothing, by finding the routines they are instances of and proving each instance against one lifted routine.

Found. Five families hold 83 of the 155: a store of one parameter into a field at a constant offset (50 instances, byte or word, four kinds of return), a copy of one static word into another (11), a comparison of a word with a constant or the parameter (6), a routine that writes constants into a few fields and returns zero, one or the object (10), and a read of a byte or word at a base plus an index times a stride (6). The other 72 are listed in groups, with the reason each is not lifted. Five of the field-store rewrites call a helper that no tracked file defines.

FactValueMeaning
Field-store instances50Byte (24) and word (26) stores; return zero, the parameter, the parameter's low byte, or nothing
Word-copy instances11One word read and one word written, return zero; fifteen static words in all
Word-test instances6Equal, not equal and signed greater, against a constant or the parameter; two read from static words
Constant-write instances10One to three constant writes of one to four bytes; return zero, one or the object
Indexed-read instances6Byte or word read at base plus index times stride, 32-bit wrapping arithmetic
Missing, does not compile5Rewrites that call a helper named wrf; no tracked file or checker runtime defines it
Lifted code addedfive modules in lf-coreNo unsafe code and no addresses; each family is one method on a small owning type with a table of instances
Proof1,000 cases per instanceResult and every byte or word the rewrite may touch compared after each call; floats compared as bits
Wrong versionsfour per family, 64 cases eachCaught by every instance in every family

Verified. In the final pass all five 32-bit test crates pass their three tests each (the differential comparison, the wrong versions, and the instance-table check); the host tests of lf-core and of the five test crates pass, and the host check of the lane's workspace passes.

Finding: the float return quiets a signalling NaN. One float-returning rewrite in the indexed-read family returned a different bit pattern from the lifted word when the entry was a signalling not-a-number: the rewrite's return passes through the floating-point return register, which sets the quiet bit. The lifted read now models that return (a float result is quieted in the same way), and the test plants signalling and quiet not-a-number patterns in each word entry. The original routine is expected to behave the same way because it returns through the same register; this is inferred from the convention, not read from the original.

Finding: five verified rewrites do not compile from the repository. The audio parameter-store rewrites call a helper named wrf. The checker index records them as verified, but no tracked file and no checker runtime defines the helper, so the test crate fails to build on them. They are listed as missing and were not worked around.

Decided. A routine whose whole content is one address behind a null check (nine rewrites) is listed, not lifted. A family of fewer than four members is listed. A read-modify-write of flag bits is listed. Every lifted method takes its object as bytes or a table, so no lifted code depends on pointer width. The tests keep indexes small enough that every read stays inside the test object; the wrap-around of the offset arithmetic is covered by host tests of the lifted method.

Process finding. Two runtime tests that share global slots raced when they ran in parallel and failed one run in several; one lock per test program fixes it. A test that compares a predicate on a random word almost never reaches the equal case: the test draws the tested word around the constant instead.

Still open. The 72 listed functions are groups, not lifts. The five wrf rewrites need the helper defined by the repository, or the rewrites changed, before they can be proven. The field-store lift is one method over a table, a weak lift: the proof shows the table describes the rewrites, not that the family's meaning is understood.

entry.title: A host for the finished game: what Bevy offers, what this engine needs, and why the renderer should be written against wgpu first
entry.summary: The owner asked, ahead of time, whether the Bevy engine should be the platform under the game once its logic exists as portable Rust, so that it can be built for many targets. Two research lanes ran side by side: one read Bevy's current state from primary sources, one measured what this engine needs from a host out of what the project already knows. This entry is the coordinator's synthesis. Nothing was installed or built for it, and the plan is unchanged until the owner decides.
entry.content:
The owner asked, ahead of time, whether the Bevy engine should be the platform under the game once its logic exists as portable Rust, so that it can be built for many targets. Two research lanes ran side by side: one read Bevy's current state from primary sources, one measured what this engine needs from a host out of what the project already knows. This entry is the coordinator's synthesis. Nothing was installed or built for it, and the plan is unchanged until the owner decides.

What was asked

Is Bevy the right host for a game that is not being designed around an entity-component system, but reproduced exactly from an existing engine with its own loop, renderer, mixer and streaming? Two uses were kept apart throughout: (A) Bevy as a platform layer only, with the game's own simulation running inside it; (B) a real port onto Bevy's entity-component system, renderer features, animation and physics.

What this engine needs from a host

AreaFindingLabel
Shaders969 distinct shader programs, all Direct3D 9 shader model 3.0. The project's own translator turns 965 of them into SPIR-V that passes its structural validator; the four that fail share one cause, an input semantic with no slot in the binding convention.Verified: the translator's test over the owner's installed files, run for this entry.
RendererA deferred pipeline: a four-target geometry buffer, stencil-masked lights, cascade and cube shadows, a high-dynamic-range post chain. Draw lists are recorded on worker threads and replayed by one render thread. Textures are block-compressed in three formats plus two uncompressed ones.Verified from earlier surveys; the draw-list structure is Likely.
AudioThe game mixes its own sound. A host has to pull samples through a callback and little else.Verified.
Threads and timeExact wait semantics for its synchronisation, a millisecond clock with its wrap behaviour, and a simulation step that follows the original's arithmetic on frame time.Verified for the calls; Likely for the step.
FilesAsynchronous, prioritised, cancellable byte-range reads into large archives, read at run time from the player's own installed copy.Verified.
Code that is not being rewrittenA compression library, an image codec and a collision library have replacements. The ragdoll behaviour middleware has no open replacement and would need a clean-room reimplementation.Verified from the library inventory.
The frame itselfThe main loop, the update order, the hand-off of draw data to the render thread and the creation of the window are in the part of the code that is encrypted on disk, which the inventory does not cover.Unknown. This is the largest gap for any host.

What Bevy offers today

QuestionFindingLabel and source
Current stateVersion 0.20 was released on 8 October 2026, on version 30 of the wgpu graphics library. Releases come every three to four months with breaking changes and migration guides; no 1.0 and no stability commitment is announced.Verified: the project's news page and release process page; the release dates were checked a second time by the coordinator.
A custom renderer inside itAn application can draw its own vertex and index buffers with its own pipeline, with none of Bevy's meshes, materials or lights; an example in the repository at the 0.20 tag shows it. The renderer can also be switched off with the window and the loop kept, and an application can own the loop. Whether an application can create its own graphics surface from Bevy's window is shown by no example.Verified from the repository's examples; the last point Unknown.
Shader inputBevy's own shader language is WGSL; support for GLSL was removed in 0.20. It accepts SPIR-V and translates it through the naga library, whose output for Metal and Direct3D 12 is a primary target and for WebGL and WebGPU a secondary one.Verified from the 0.20 documentation and migration guide.
Reading the game's dataA custom asset source is supported, with an asynchronous, seekable reader. The documented contract of a read is a whole file; ranged reads into a multi-gigabyte container during play are not documented either way.Verified from the documentation; the fit is Unknown until tested.
PlatformsDesktop Linux, macOS, iOS and Android are listed as supported by the project's own example tester; Windows on Direct3D 12 and the web are listed as in progress. The project's continuous integration has no Windows target for ARM64 processors. The one report for that platform is an open rendering fault on a Qualcomm integrated graphics processor under Vulkan, opened in June 2026, with no maintainer reply. No console support is documented.Verified: the example tester page and the issue, which the coordinator also read.
PrecedentsThe closest found is a rewrite of an older shooter's engine on Bevy, whose author kept the world and client state in one central structure and wrote most of the rendering by hand against wgpu. No reimplementation of an older open-world game on Bevy or on wgpu in Rust was found.Verified from that project's own description; the absence is as far as two searches went.
AlternativesThe windowing library and wgpu that Bevy itself is built on can be used directly with the project's own loop. SDL 3 reaches consoles, but only through ports under a non-disclosure agreement. Fyrox reached 1.0 in September 2026. Godot can host Rust through bindings, with consoles through a commercial third party.Verified for versions and dates; the console terms from the projects' own pages.

The coordinator's reading

This part is judgement, not finding.

  • Use (B), a port onto Bevy's entity-component system and its own renderer, animation and physics, has no case here. The project's rule is exact reproduction of the original's behaviour, and each of those subsystems would replace something that is being reproduced. The one precedent found made the same choice for the same reason.
  • Use (A), Bevy as a platform layer, is feasible: its custom-pass route, its acceptance of SPIR-V and its optional renderer cover what the engine needs. What it costs is exposure to a renderer interface that changed in each of the last two releases, a platform (Windows on ARM64, which is the owner's own machine) that the project does not test, and no route to consoles.
  • The renderer should be written against wgpu directly, as a crate of its own, and not against Bevy's rendering interface. Bevy is built on the same library, so the same passes would run inside a Bevy application or inside a bare window-and-loop shell, and the choice of shell stays reversible behind the platform traits the lifted crates already use. The translated shaders enter the same way in both.
  • Web and mobile are limited less by the host than by the data: the game's files must come from the player's own copy, which on the web means a file the player selects, and the block-compressed textures are not usable as they are on most mobile graphics processors.

What was decided

Nothing yet beyond recording this. Two questions are with the owner: whether a lane may fetch the Bevy and wgpu crates for an experiment kept outside the main workspace (the project's rule is that nothing is downloaded without his approval), and whether a host-platform phase goes into the plan.

The experiment proposed, with its pass criteria stated in advance: one section of the map, parsed by the project's own loaders, drawn with one translated shader through passes written against wgpu, once inside a Bevy 0.20 application and once in a bare shell, on the owner's ARM64 Windows machine and on an x86-64 one. It passes if the draw is correct on both machines, the shaders compile on Direct3D 12 and on Vulkan, and the archive is read by ranges without copying the container.

How to reproduce it

The shader figure comes from the translator crate's test over real files, which runs when the game folder's location is given in the environment and is skipped otherwise; it reads the shader containers and writes nothing. The engine's requirements are queries over the project's evidence database and the earlier devlog entries on the executable, the formats and the shaders. The Bevy findings each carry their source in the research lane's report, one hundred sources in all, of which this entry links the two the coordinator read again.

entry.title: A contract that set its globals in the wrong place, and how many others may have
entry.summary: A lane that was sent to make the checker observe one float comparison could not, and reported that the checker was not applying two values its contract set. The checker was applying them exactly where the contract said. The contract said the wrong place.
entry.content:
A lane that was sent to make the checker observe one float comparison could not, and reported that the checker was not applying two values its contract set. The checker was applying them exactly where the contract said. The contract said the wrong place.

What was asked

Why do two globals that a proof's contract sets, a divisor and a size, read back as minus one on both sides whatever value the contract gives them? And if a contract can be wrong in this way without anything noticing, how many are?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Where the contract of record puts the two valuesAt addresses a fixed amount below the globals the function reads, inside the code section. Verified.An arithmetic slip when the lane turned an address in the image into an offset from the image base. The worker writes the values there; the function never reads them; both sides read the file's own value of the real globals, which is minus one.
What the proof of record then coveredA grid whose index never leaves zero. It passes 1,000 of 1,000 trials. Verified by reproducing it with an instrumented copy.The proof is real and says much less than it appears to: the part of the function that divides, rounds and indexes was never exercised with a usable divisor.
The same contract with the two addresses correctedThe verified rewrite fails 30 of 1,000 trials; with a positive divisor and size, 85 of 1,000. A copy with one float comparison corrected passes. Verified on the stock worker with an unchanged copy of the driver; the lane wrote its predictions down before running.The rewrite was wrong: a rounding helper compares with "not less than" where the original's instruction is "not less than or equal", which differ for whole-number inputs. An audit had read that from the instruction earlier in the day and could not show it. The rewrite had already been withdrawn on the ground that its proof did not reach the code in doubt; that is now a shown difference.
A deliberately wrong version on the corrected contractFails 494 of 1,000. Verified.The corrected contract sees the code. Under the contract of record a wrong version of that code would have passed.
Contracts of record scanned for the condition16,381 read; 238 functions have no contract file where the index says and were not scanned.The scan follows each verified function to its proving lane's contract; it does not search.
Contracts that place a value or a range in code54 functions.Certain faults in the contract: nothing is ever meant to be set there. Each of those proofs is narrower than it says. Whether the rewrite is right on the wider input is not yet known for any of them.
Contracts that set words the function's body never refers to738 functions, 5,674 words.Some are slips of the same kind, some are values meant for a callee, some are an image address written where an offset is wanted. Not yet separated.
Functions that write to data the contract neither declares nor compares in full148.A rewrite could write something different there and no check would see it.
Functions with the same signature as the one that started this288. In a sample of ten read by hand, nine of the values gate a branch, index a table, feed arithmetic or reach an unchecked output; one is harmless. Inferred from reading listings.The condition usually matters where it occurs.

Correction to an earlier statement

The lane that first met this wrote that the checker does not apply a contract's values at those two addresses. That was wrong, and the changelog entry of the withdrawal repeated the doubt. The checker writes a value where the contract names it and checks nothing about whether that is a place the function reads. That is the gap: not a fault in what the checker does, but something it never looked at.

What was decided

  • The rewrite stays withdrawn and a strengthening lane is proving the corrected copy, with every other address in its contract checked the same way.
  • The investigation lane continues from counting to measuring: for the 54 certain cases first, then the 148, it corrects the contract and runs the verified rewrite through it on the stock checker. A rewrite that then fails on trials the original completes is withdrawn; one that still passes gets the corrected contract as its contract of record.
  • The lane wrote a check for the driver that refuses a contract which places a value outside writable data, with tests. It will be adopted in a narrower form: a refusal for code, gaps and addresses outside the image, which can never be meant; a warning for read-only data, because varying a constant the original loads from there is a legitimate test and one the day's other findings call for; and a verdict file that records the refusal.
  • The production brief will tell lanes how to turn an image address into the offset a contract wants, to check that every address they set is one the function's body refers to, and to confirm with a deliberately wrong version that each value they set is seen.

How to reproduce it

For a contract, take every address it sets or declares and find the section of the image it falls in; then decode the function and list the absolute data addresses its instructions refer to. An address the contract sets that is in code, or that no instruction of the function refers to, is a candidate. The lane's script does this for one contract or for the whole verified set and writes the list.

entry.title: Head-swap and constant-store families: 170 instances proven against two lifted methods
entry.summary: From lane l-free21.
entry.content:
From lane l-free21.

Asked. Lift a group of 198 verified 21-byte functions that call nothing, by finding the data they share and lifting each shape once.

Found. Most of the group is one routine: read a global list head, store the old value into a second word, point the head at a static node, and return the old value. One hundred and sixty-two rewrites have this shape. Eight more write two constants into two global words and return zero or nothing. The other 28 members are different shapes (branching readers, bit tests on a record, clears and copies through a record pointer) and are listed, not lifted.

FactValueMeaning
Head-swap members162Verified rewrites with one head read, one save write, one head write to a node, and a return of the read value
Textual groups11 for the same routineA hash of the normalised text splits one routine into eleven groups; extracting the roles of each rewrite groups them correctly
Constant-store members8Two constants written to two global words, returns zero (seven) or nothing (one)
Lifted code addedtwo methods in one new moduleOne list-head method and one two-word store, with no unsafe code and no addresses
Proof170 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery returned value and every word compared, rebuilt through the same addresses
Wrong versionshead left unchanged; save takes the node; a store left outCaught for every instance

Verified. The four test crates pass on the 32-bit target (59, 59, 47 and 9 tests, none failing). The 64-bit workspace check and the host edge tests pass.

Decided. Prove the list family as one method on a table of link words, with words named by index, rather than as a class. The store-order version of the list routine is equivalent on every input the instances can reach, because the save word and the head are always different words. It is asserted to agree, and it is not counted as a caught wrong version.

Process finding. A differential test shows a wrong version is caught only if it can differ on a reachable input. Any order-only mutant over distinct words is equivalent, so the next brief should name that case instead of requiring a catch.

Still open. The 28 odd members need separate lifts with their own proofs. The return value of the constant-store family is checked by the test, not carried by the lifted method.

entry.title: Quotient-store family: 229 more instances proven against one lifted routine
entry.summary: From lane l-free20.
entry.content:
From lane l-free20.

Asked. Lift a group of 265 verified 25-byte functions that call nothing, by finding the data they share and lifting each instance family once.

Found. Most of the group is one routine: read two single-precision globals, divide, and store the quotient in a third global. Two hundred and twenty-nine rewrites have this shape. Their return is absent, a dead integer zero, or the stored quotient. The other 36 members are different shapes (branching accessors, pointer-arithmetic setters, store-only copies) and are listed, not lifted.

FactValueMeaning
Members of the routine229Verified rewrites with one division, two global reads, one global write
Return kinds125 none, 85 dead zero, 19 quotientThe dead return is checked to be zero and not compared further
Lifted code addednoneThe existing quotient routine in the vehicle module is proven for each instance
Proof229 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery effect compared bit for bit, including sources and not-a-number payloads
Wrong versionsoperands swapped, wrong destinationBoth caught for every instance

Verified. All four test crates pass on the 32-bit target. A deliberately swapped lift fails 58 of 58 instances in one batch. The 64-bit host edge tests (7) pass.

Decided. Prove the instances against the existing routine rather than write a second copy. Batches are at most 58 rewrites per test crate. Non-vehicle instances are tested against the vehicle module for now; a move to a neutral module is a coordinator decision.

Process finding. A copy of a tracked source into a build tree keeps its old modification time, and cargo then reuses a stale binary. The generator now gives copies a new time. Any future generator that copies sources must do the same.

Still open. Six flag-gated field setters depend on a shared record lookup that is not a verified function. They wait until that lookup is verified.

entry.title: One red pipeline run, three causes, and a fourth thing it uncovered: 706 verified rewrites whose published file is not the code that was proven
entry.summary: The pipeline on the public repository failed on an afternoon commit after passing all morning. The failing jobs had three unrelated causes, two of them faults in the project's own tooling, and following the third to its end showed that 3.7% of the verified rewrites cannot be built into the assembled library from the file that is published for them.
entry.content:
The pipeline on the public repository failed on an afternoon commit after passing all morning. The failing jobs had three unrelated causes, two of them faults in the project's own tooling, and following the third to its end showed that 3.7% of the verified rewrites cannot be built into the assembled library from the file that is published for them.

What was asked

Why did a commit that only added three lifted routines break the job that assembles every verified rewrite into one library, and the job that checks the rewrite tree against its index?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Index rows lostFive verified rewrites had a file and no row in the index. Verified.Three finishers and the coordinator ran the importer at the same moment. Each read the index, added its rows and wrote the whole file back; the last writer's copy dropped the others' rows. The fault was on the safe side, verified work not counted, and the consistency check caught it within the hour.
Files the assembler dropped on the failing commit35 in one shard, of which 5 were at fault. Verified by replaying the shard locally.When a shard fails to build, the assembler reads the compiler's messages and drops the rewrites they point at. It took any position in a file named lib.rs to be in the shard's own root file. The checker runtime's export macro lives in a file of the same name, so an error reached through the macro was looked up by line number in the wrong file and blamed on a rewrite that compiles. Each round dropped another innocent file, the two that really failed were never dropped, and after 30 rounds the job gave up.
Had the assembler done this before?Unknown. The earlier manifests are not kept.Earlier passing runs may have left out rewrites that compile. It cost nothing but their place in the library, and the next run includes them.
Verified rewrites left out of the assembled library, with the assembler corrected706 of 19,026. Verified from the manifest of the first passing run.472 do not compile on their own and 234 are refused before compiling. This is the finding that matters.
Why the 472 do not compile248 call a function that is not in the file, 72 use a constant and 64 a type that is not there, 13 import something that does not exist, 18 use a reserved word as a name, 13 have an unclosed bracket, 7 define a name twice, 3 define a second panic handler.A lane proves a function with a library built from its own crate, where helpers, constants and types may sit in a shared module. Only the one file is published. In two cases the published file is a three-line wrapper and the whole body stayed in the lane's folder.
Why the 234 are refused206 use a runtime of the lane's own in place of the shared one, 17 have no export the assembler recognises, 5 still carry a wrong version beside the right one.Mostly early lanes, from before the shared runtime was the rule.
When they were proven346 on the second checker version, 213 recorded on the current one.128 of the 213 are old files whose proofs the regression lanes have re-run; 85 come from production and queue lanes working on the current checker. It is still happening, slowly.

What this does and does not say

It does not say these 706 rewrites are wrong. Each passed its trials, with its wrong version rejected where the checker version required one, as a library built by its lane. What it says is narrower and still serious: for these functions the file in the repository is not the thing the checker ran. The coordinator's independent re-run has the same blind spot, because it runs the lane's built library and never builds the published file. A reader who takes the published file as the verified code is, for 3.7% of the set, reading something that does not build.

What was decided

  • The importer and the withdrawal script now hold one lock from reading the index to writing it. The five rows are restored.
  • The assembler counts an error position only when it is in the shard's own root file or the shard's own copy of a rewrite, with three tests. On the failing commit it then drops exactly the files that do not compile and builds in two rounds. The pipeline passes again.
  • The 706 stay counted as verified for now, with this entry as the statement of what that count includes. A tool lane is classifying them by what a repair takes, writing a check the importer can run on every file before it is published (does it compile alone, against the shared runtime, as the assembler would place it), repairing two of each class from the proving lane's own source and proving each repaired file by building it alone and running the contract of record against that build. What a script can repair is repaired by script; the rest goes to lanes; what cannot be made whole is proven again.
  • Once that check exists, a published file that does not compile on its own is held at import with the reason, and the production brief says so.

How to reproduce it

The assembled library's manifest is an artifact of every pipeline run: its excluded list has one record per file left out, with the stage and the compiler's first message. Grouping that list by message gives the table above. The assembler's fault is covered by the tests added with the correction: an error reached through the runtime's macro is attributed to the rewrite it came from and not to the rewrite that owns the same line number in the shard.

Update, the same evening: 706 down to 218

The tool lane classified the 706, repaired by script what a script could repair from the proving lanes' own source, and wrote a prover that needs no model: it builds each repaired file alone and runs the proving lane's contract of record against that build on the stock checker, with the lane's wrong version where one exists. Of 550 repaired files it settled, 501 pass: 130 with their wrong version rejected, 371 where the proving lane has no wrong version that can still be run. 488 of them replaced their published files in two commits, after the coordinator checked each file's hash against the prover's record and that the set builds alone. The next pipeline run assembled 19,414 of 19,632 verified rewrites and left out 218, where the run before the repair left out 706 of 19,593. Verified.

The importer now runs the same build-alone check on every claim before it is published, and a claim whose file fails is held with the compiler's reason. What remains of the 218: files that call a helper or use a type no script could trace to a definition, 18 that use a word the current language edition reserves, 9 on a lane runtime whose repair is not a pure renaming, and 8 with no export the assembler recognises. They go to lanes.

entry.title: Widening a proof's inputs: seven verified rewrites differed from the original, and only four were the fault being looked for
entry.summary: An audit that began with one question, how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, ended the day as a general test: take a verified rewrite and its contract of record, widen the contract so that every float the function can read takes extreme values on a share of trials, and run it again on the stock checker. Seven rewrites that had passed their proofs differ from the original under that test, on trials the original completes.
