Indirect calls through a vtable can be scripted by planting a stub in a heap vtable, and in a game vtable slot through the globals listVerifiedThe eight indirect sites of the function run through one stub id; the game's own vtable code is never executed.
Whole-function rewrite with 35 callee ids passes six stock-v8 contractsVerified1,000 of 1,000 positives on each, with a same-contract wrong version failing 3 of 3 for each.

Decided. Encrypted callees are handled by stubs exactly like plain callees. A capture is needed only if a callee's real behaviour must be proven, which a stub never does. The earlier deferral's reason, that the mapped image is ciphertext at the callee, is correct about the bytes but was not a blocker for the checker. The function is recorded as verified with its narrowed list (stub semantics, null-receiver fault paths not proven).

Reproduce. Patch each direct call instruction of the function (its relative address in the image) to a scripted callee id in the contract, and plant the stub in each indirect target slot. Run the stock checker in a 60-trial probe: the original reports ok, orig_ok equal to the trial count.

Limits: the proof covers the function under the stub model only; a callee's real effects on its pointer arguments are not compared.

Written by lane a-H01; integrated by the coordinator.

entry.title: The checker's option for unrelocated absolute reads has never set up on this machine
entry.summary: The checker has a contract option for an original that reads an absolute address which the loader did not relocate: the worker holds the address range of the original's preferred base, so such a read lands on a copy of the image. A lane on a large function asked for the option, was refused, and reported that the repository's own self-test contract for it fails the same way. A checker investigation lane took 15 minutes to settle it. The option fails at set-up on this machine every time, it has done so since the day it was added, and nothing a lane can do changes that.
entry.content:
The checker has a contract option for an original that reads an absolute address which the loader did not relocate: the worker holds the address range of the original's preferred base, so such a read lands on a copy of the image. A lane on a large function asked for the option, was refused, and reported that the repository's own self-test contract for it fails the same way. A checker investigation lane took 15 minutes to settle it. The option fails at set-up on this machine every time, it has done so since the day it was added, and nothing a lane can do changes that.

What was asked

Is the refusal a fault in the checker, a fault in the lane's contract, or the machine? Twenty deferred functions, 27,343 bytes, were queued behind this option, so the answer mattered beyond one lane.

What was found

QuestionFindingHow it is known
Does the self-test contract fail?Yes, at set-up, before any trial: 10 of 10 fresh driver runs, 40 of 40 set-up attempts counting the driver's own retries.Verified: run on the stock driver and worker.
What holds the range?One block mapped by the system, present at the first line of the worker's own code, covering the whole range. It is not the worker's image, which sits elsewhere. None of the 768 pieces of the range can be reserved, and the block cannot be released.Verified: a private copy of the worker that lists the regions in the range before it reserves anything.
Does it depend on how the worker is linked?The layout changes and the outcome does not. Linked at a fixed base, as the worker is, the block is always there. Linked to load at a random base, some pieces of the range are free on some starts, never all of them: 0 of 40 set-ups.Verified: two small 32-bit probe programs, one linked each way.
Is it new?No. The first lane log that records the worker holding none of the range is from 4 October, the day the option went live. Forty-one lane logs record a deferral for it since. No log of a contract passing with the option was found on this machine.Verified for the logs; that it never passed is inferred from finding none.
Does it depend on load, or on how the worker is started?No: the same with 25 other workers running and with none started by the driver.Verified.
Would it work after a restart, or on a machine with an x86 processor?Unknown. This machine runs 32-bit x86 code under emulation, which may be what maps the block; that was not tested.Unknown.

Repairs tried and ruled out: linking the worker differently, reserving earlier (the block is there before the worker runs), releasing the block, and retrying. Covering only the pieces that can be held was not tried, on purpose: the worker refuses a partial cover by design, because a read that lands on a piece it does not hold would silently read the worker's own memory.

What was decided

  • No lane is sent at a contract that needs this option, or at its self-test contract. The self-test's failure is a known condition of this machine, not a regression in the checker.
  • The twenty queued functions stay deferred with this as the stated reason. Before any of them is believed to need the option, its claim is checked with the relocation checker: an earlier devlog entry records that every such claim examined so far was wrong, and the worker already relocates absolute immediates so that most data reads work without the option (see the entry of 5 October on a production lane).
  • Getting the option to work is a design change to the checker, for the owner to decide: for example loading the original at its preferred base in a process built for that purpose. It is not a lane repair.

Correction

Lane notes since 4 October say the range is taken "in every 32-bit process". That is true only of programs linked at a fixed base. It does not change the outcome, and it is corrected here so the next investigation does not start from it.

How to reproduce

Run the self-test contract for the option from the checker's contract folder on the stock driver, ten times, each in a fresh driver process, and read the set-up message. The investigation lane's commands, outputs and the region listings are in its scratch folder.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 11 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour. Since this night the review runs from its own timer on a checklist the owner supplied, and starts from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in "Hourly reviews, 10 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour. Since this night the review runs from its own timer on a checklist the owner supplied, and starts from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in "Hourly reviews, 10 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:20First review on the owner's checklist. In the 1.2 hours since 23:05: verified code up by 10,098 bytes in 11 functions imported after re-run (8,300 bytes an hour), nothing withdrawn, no portable lift, and 3,503 functions named, which took the named count from 32,227 to 35,730 of 37,413. The owner lifted the lane limit twice in the hour, first for naming and then for all Luna lanes, down to 2 GB of spare memory: the lane count went from 12 to 67. No lane stalled. Four Haiku lanes on large functions ended, each further along and none closed, and were continued by fresh lanes from their kits, except a 5,042-byte function that has had three sessions and is parked for a stronger lane. Every imported claim held on the re-run. Blockers, in order: the processor, at its ceiling for the whole hour with up to 21 compilers and 23 checker workers at once, so that a status command took ten minutes; the pipeline on the public repository, failing since 8 October; large functions, of which 384 of 1,807 of 1,000 bytes and more are verified and each takes several lane sessions; and the trust backlog, with 11% of the verified functions recorded on the current checker.The review got its own timer and a scorecard script, and the checklist went into the agent rules. Production brief version b24: a call into the part of the program encrypted on disk, or through a pointer, is replaced by a stand-in, not deferred (eight of one batch's seventeen functions had been deferred for it). A repair lane was put on the pipeline's two failures and a lift lane was started, the first since 6 October. The runaway guard was taught to recognise a script started by a lane's agent, and stopped seven over 3 GB. A filler starts Luna lanes while memory allows and the supervisor finishes them. Verified bytes per hour rose from about 4,300 to 8,300 while lanes rose fivefold: the extra lanes pay much less than in proportion.
01:25The best hour since work resumed. In 1.1 hours: verified code up by 14,183 bytes in 105 functions (13,500 bytes an hour, against 8,300 the hour before and 615 over the last 58 hours), five more routines lifted to portable Rust, 273 more functions named (36,003 of 37,413). The pipeline on the public repository passed for the first time since 8 October: a repair lane found both causes (a test received Python's own queue module because a checker import left it in the module cache; a lift test crate included a rewrite that had been withdrawn) and the coordinator tested and installed its candidates. Haiku lanes closed two more large functions, of 3,313 and 2,215 bytes, which makes four tonight; in the second the lane first showed, with realistic output values, that the earlier rewrite was wrong, then corrected and proved it. By model, for lanes that ended in the hour: Luna, 121 functions and 30,041 bytes in 19.7 lane-hours, 1,524 bytes per lane-hour; Haiku, 5,528 bytes in 3.0 lane-hours, 1,831 per lane-hour, all of it in functions Luna's lanes had left partly proven. Proof integrity: the re-run held eleven claims of one Luna lane, and that was the re-run's fault for the third time tonight: one slow contract ran the batch of fifteen into its time limit and the ten after it were never run. Run one at a time, all seventeen hold. Deferrals: 31 with the reason given only as "other" and 21 for time, in lanes that are slowed by the load. Three Luna lanes had written nothing for over twenty minutes; they run below normal priority and are slow, not stopped.Fixed in the hour. Every Luna lane's processes run below normal priority, so the steps that turn finished work into counted work get the processor first: thirteen finished lanes had been waiting, two for over half an hour, and the backlog cleared within minutes. Commits go one at a time and each takes only its own paths, after a pipeline repair went into the history inside an import commit that happened at the same moment. The re-run runs one contract per driver process with its own time limit, reports a missing verdict as its own failure, accepts a contract without a wrong version when the lane's other contracts reject theirs, and takes a wrong version as equivalent only when the coordinator has recorded why. Next, with owners: the two large functions still partly proven (fresh Haiku lanes when the load allows; the 5,042-byte one waits for a stronger lane); the deferrals marked "other" (the coordinator reads a sample before the next review and the brief gets the missing reasons); the 14,997 proofs still to re-run on the current checker (nine Luna lanes running); one verified function whose contract and rewrite disagree about the register a callee's result is read from, found by the lift lane (a checker-reading lane). Accelerating: yes, against both the previous hour and the baseline, with the lane count unchanged from the hour before; the gain came from clearing the finishing backlog, not from more lanes.
02:05Scorecard for the 0.7 hours since 01:25: verified code up by 14,152 bytes in 155 functions (17,262 verified; 21,200 bytes an hour against 13,500 the hour before and 850 over the last 58 hours), no lift, 27 functions named, nothing withdrawn, the pipeline passing, no lane stalled, 4.0 GB of memory available. Throughput in total is up; throughput per lane has collapsed. The 56 Luna lanes that ended in the last 65 minutes verified 253 functions and 38,200 bytes in 80.4 lane-hours: 475 bytes per lane-hour, against 1,524 the hour before and about 4,000 when twelve lanes ran. Small-function lanes finished 27% of their batches (175 of 637): 250 functions were not reached and 123 were deferred for time, in lanes that each get a small share of a saturated processor (18 logical processors, about sixty lanes with up to three checker workers each). Another 100 deferrals gave the reason only as "other"; read, most are lanes that counted every checker worker on the machine against a limit of three meant for their own, and did not run the checker at all. Queue lanes had also been handed the same functions several times over: thirty lanes, fourteen distinct functions. Proof integrity: the re-run held two claims of one Luna lane, and this time the finding is real: run again by hand, the original faults on a fifth of the trials where the rewrite returns normally, 60 and 67 of 300. Those two stay out. They are the first Luna claims that do not reproduce, 2 of about 550 tonight. Haiku: two more large functions closed in the window; one lane on a function whose main loop is still unmapped proved four stages and then declined the loop twice, the third function tonight where that happened.Changed in the hour. The limit of three checker workers is stated as a lane's own in the agent rules and in brief version b25, and the 68 functions left drafted and untested got a queue of their own, with five lanes on them. The queue brief maker counts the Luna queue series as taken; the ten duplicate lanes still running were stopped. The re-run takes the newest library that actually holds the function's export, after two lanes' claims could not be re-run. New Luna starts are paused and the count is left to fall from about sixty to thirty. The owner's instruction was to fill memory to within 2 GB; the reason to depart from it is in the numbers above and in the project's own record, whose best hour (56,000 bytes) was made with 28 lanes, and one word from him restores it. Next, with owners: the two claims that do not reproduce go back to the pool with the re-run's finding (Luna); a lane with one narrow step, a probe that settles where the stack frame starts, for the function whose loop was declined (Haiku); the 14,702 proofs still to re-run on the current checker (Luna, ten lanes running); the next review compares bytes per hour and per lane-hour at the lower count. Accelerating in total, yes; per lane, no, and the per-lane figure is the one that says whether the machine is being used well.
03:00Scorecard for the 0.9 hours since 02:05: verified code up by 17,653 bytes in 108 functions (17,370 verified; 19,300 bytes an hour against 21,200 the hour before), no lift, nothing withdrawn, the pipeline passing, no lane stalled, 9.1 GB of memory available. New Luna starts have been paused since 02:06 and the count fell from about sixty to 33; total output per hour stayed about level while lanes halved, which is the answer to whether the extra lanes were adding anything. Output per lane-hour is still low, 404 bytes, because the lanes ending in this hour all started in the crowd: small-function lanes finished a quarter of their batches (83 of 335, with 163 not reached and 44 out of time). One lane that started after the worker rule was corrected verified 23 of 23. Proof integrity: nothing held this hour; 19% of the verified functions are now recorded on the current checker (3,303 of 17,475), up from 15%. Haiku: four lanes ended on large functions, none closed, all further along. A lane given one narrow job, to settle a function's stack frame by experiment, did it in 17 minutes where the lane before had declined the function's loop twice; the frame disagreement that stopped the earlier lane turned out not to exist. One function is at 32 stage contracts on one rewrite after four sessions and a few named routes from done; another went from 11 to 18 stages and its lane found a latent error in an inherited stage. Deferrals: 70 for time and 67 marked other, both from lanes started in the crowd.Changed in the hour: the re-run handles a contract whose name cannot be a file name; a finished lane whose leftover monitors kept waking it was stopped. For large functions the method is now explicit: where the routes are mapped, a fresh lane gets the remaining routes as an ordered list of small steps; where a body is unmapped, a lane gets one narrow job (a probe, a frame map, one pass built call by call against a prepared probe) and is not asked to finish the function. Next: when the filler's window ends in a few minutes it is restarted with a ceiling of thirty Luna lanes and the pause is lifted, so that lanes started at the lower count, on the corrected brief, can be measured; the 04:05 review compares their yield per lane-hour with tonight's. Owners: Luna for small functions, the re-runs of old proofs (14,172 left) and the drafted-but-untested queue; Haiku for the three large functions in hand. Accelerating: level with the previous hour in total at half the lanes, and well above the baseline.
04:05The best hour of the night, at half the lanes. In the 1.1 hours since 03:00: verified code up by 55,828 bytes in 403 functions (17,773 verified; 51,500 bytes an hour, against 19,300 the hour before), nothing withdrawn, nothing held on the re-run, the pipeline passing, no lane stalled, 9.3 GB of memory available. The Luna count was held at thirty for the whole hour. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 404 functions and 51,941 bytes in 51.2 lane-hours, 1,015 bytes per lane-hour against 404 the hour before; small-function lanes finished 59% of their batches against 25%. Lanes started after the count came down and the worker rule was corrected finished full or nearly full batches (28 of 28, 27 of 28, 28 of 30, 23 of 23), and the queue of functions that had been drafted and never run is paying: 28 of 28 in one lane. The hour's figure includes work from lanes that ended earlier and waited to be counted, so the next hour is the cleaner measure. Haiku closed its fifth large function of the night, 4,512 bytes, in five sessions; the coordinator's re-run passed all 70 of its contracts, and three stage variants whose wrong version cannot be seen on that variant are recorded as not counted, with the reason. A second function is one branch from whole: the branch had been taken for a fault in the checker, and a checker investigation lane showed in 16 minutes that it was the contract: a scripted write through a pointer counts words, and the contract asked for eight through a pointer to a two-word local. Recorded on the current checker: 23% of the verified functions, up from 19%. Deferrals for time fell from 70 to 39.Kept: thirty Luna lanes. The owner's instruction was to fill memory; the measured result of holding at thirty is more than twice the output of sixty, and it stays at thirty unless he says otherwise. Changed in the hour: a second finisher works the list of ended lanes from the other end, with each lane claimed before it is worked on, after eleven finished lanes had been waiting for one finisher; the re-run records, with a reason, stage contracts whose wrong version is not rejected and which the lane itself does not count. For large functions three briefing forms are now in use and each has closed work tonight: an ordered list of small routes where the function is mapped; one narrow job where it is not (a frame map, one loop pass or one block built call by call against a prepared probe); and a checker investigation when a lane reports a checker fault, before anyone believes it. Next, with owners: the last branch of the 3,440-byte function (Haiku, running); the block three routes converge on in the 3,422-byte function (Haiku, running); a lift lane on one narrow data shape, since no lift ran this hour (Haiku, started with this review); 13,808 proofs still to re-run on the current checker (Luna, four lanes). Accelerating: yes, against the previous hour and the baseline.
05:05A steadier hour, and two faults found in the coordinator's own tooling. In the hour since 04:05: verified code up by 24,334 bytes in 129 functions (17,902 verified; 25,200 bytes an hour, against 51,500 the hour before, which had counted lanes waiting from earlier, and 19,300 the hour before that), nothing withdrawn, nothing held on the re-run, the pipeline passing, 10 GB of memory available. Thirty Luna lanes throughout. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 150 functions and 35,137 bytes in 15.1 lane-hours, 2,331 bytes per lane-hour against 1,015 the hour before. Haiku closed its sixth large function of the night, 3,440 bytes, and the way it closed is the hour's lesson: the lane reported it verified while listing, as a limitation, that a version with one subtraction reversed still passed. Sent back to find out why, it found in six minutes that its contracts had placed a table of floats at the wrong address, so the table read as zero on both sides and the whole product it feeds was multiplied by nothing. All 47 contracts were corrected, the reversed version is caught, and the coordinator's re-run holds. A wrong version that passes is never a limitation to list. A portable lift of 23 routines was integrated (four data shapes, 43 differential tests, 39 wrong versions caught); the lane reached 27 of the 149 functions sharing a name prefix, which were at least seven unrelated shapes. Recorded on the current checker: 24% of the verified functions, 13,727 still to re-run. Functions of 1,000 bytes and more: 398 of 1,807 verified.Fixed in the hour: the watchdog that stops processes left behind by ended lanes was also stopping the coordinator's own re-run of an ended lane's proofs, because the re-run names the lane's contract; it broke one lane's re-run twice (nothing was imported and nothing held, and the lane is being re-run), and it explains the re-runs that broke without cause earlier in the night. Changed: the queue of functions drafted and never run is empty, so its slot goes to the queue of functions that ran out of time (295 functions, nothing blocking them). The three blockers. First, the processor, at 100% all hour with 10 GB of memory unused: finishing one lane took the supervisor up to sixteen minutes. Second, the re-run of old proofs on the current checker: six lanes tonight settled 27 to 95 proofs each of 350 in a hundred minutes, about 80 an hour for the project, because each lane writes its own preparation, build and run scripts first and then waits for the processor; at that rate the backlog is a week. This is scripted work that needs no model, so a tool lane now builds one resumable runner from those lanes' scripts, for the coordinator to run in the background; lanes then take only the proofs that fail. Third, the large functions: 118 partly proven ones hold 192,000 bytes, and three Haiku lanes close about one an hour. Kept: thirty Luna lanes. Next, with owners: the regression runner (Haiku tool lane, started with this review); three large functions in progress (Haiku); the lane count against the processor is the owner's decision and is put to him. Accelerating against the baseline; level with the average of the last three hours.
06:05The hour's work was on the re-run of old proofs, and it found the process had been quietly running out of work it could see. In the hour since 05:05: verified code up by 33,808 bytes in 270 functions (18,172 verified; 33,300 bytes an hour against 25,200 the hour before), nothing withdrawn, nothing held on the re-run, the pipeline passing, 8 GB of memory available, thirty Luna lanes. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 352 functions and 41,297 bytes in 38.5 lane-hours, 1,071 bytes per lane-hour. No large function closed in the hour: two went from 8 to 23 and from 33 to 41 proven stages and stay partly proven, and a third was reported verified with seven branches unwritten and was sent back; five of the seven turned out to be paths on which the original itself faults, the other two are now written and proven. The tool lane delivered a regression runner in 43 minutes: a script that rebuilds tracked rewrites in small crates, re-runs each proof of record unchanged on the current checker with its saved wrong version, and can be stopped and resumed. On 123 functions every outcome was a hold with the wrong version rejected, at about 13 seconds a function with three workers, against about 80 proofs an hour from all the regression lanes together. Wiring it in showed three things. The list maker counted every proof ever handed to a regression lane as taken for good, and lanes reached 27 to 95 of the 350 each was given: it reported 1,636 proofs left of 13,700. Proofs first recorded on checker versions 1 to 4 (5,395 functions) have no saved wrong version: of 350 of them, 83 passed unchanged and wait only for a wrong version to be written. And 257 of those 350 did not build in the tool for one missing import, a gap in the tool and not in the rewrites.Fixed in the hour: the list maker gives out again what an ended lane did not reach (6,857 proofs available where it saw 1,636); the runner's crates import the runtime's names the way the first weeks' proving crates did; and the runner records what it cannot settle as not reached, with the reason, after its first list would have put 348 verified functions into the deferral queues as if they had failed (corrected before anything imported it). The runner now works through the proofs recorded on versions 5 to 7 (5,599, all with saved wrong versions) with three workers and no model. A Haiku lane that had produced nothing for 24 minutes, with no process of its own alive, was stopped and resumed with its context. The three blockers. First, the processor, still at 100% with memory to spare. Second, the 5,395 old proofs without a wrong version: the runner can do the build and the thousand trials, and a lane then only writes the wrong version; the brief for that kind of lane is next. Third, the large functions: Haiku lanes add stages steadily and close few; three lanes are on three functions with ordered lists. No lift ran in the hour, for want of a lane and not for a blocker: a lift lane is started with this review on the 118 functions the last one did not reach. Kept: thirty Luna lanes. Accelerating against the baseline and against the previous hour.
15:20Eight hours with nothing verified, because the machine was asleep for six and a half of them. The 07:05 review had measured the hour before (verified code up by 17,550 bytes in 75 functions, half the hour before it, with the processor shared between thirty production lanes, twelve naming lanes, five Haiku lanes and the new regression runner at normal priority) and was being acted on when the coordinator's turn was cut off. With the coordinator idle the request that keeps the machine awake lapsed, and the machine went into standby at 07:06. It woke at 11:33, when every background window ended at once and four Haiku lanes failed for want of a network, slept again from 13:06, and woke at 15:16. Between 07:04 and 15:18: no function verified, none named, none lifted, nothing withdrawn. The regression runner finished its list across the gap: of 350 proofs first recorded on checker version 5, 311 hold with their saved wrong version rejected, 33 have no saved wrong version, 5 could not run and 1 fails. The 38 Luna lanes survived the standby and resumed by themselves; they are hours past their deadlines by the clock and are closing. One large function (4,490 bytes) had been reported verified before the gap; the coordinator's first re-run held it for a reason of form (its wrong versions are kept as contracts of their own, which the re-run read as failing claims), the rule was corrected to recognise such pairs by content, and the second re-run was cut by the standby.Recovered in the first minutes: the request to stay awake renewed; supervisor, filler, both guards, finisher and registry restarted; the four Haiku lanes resumed with their context and new deadlines; the re-run of the large function and the import of the regression list restarted, with the regression loop to follow. Changed: the regression runner now runs below normal priority like the Luna lanes, after its first hour at normal priority coincided with the halving of new verified code. The three blockers. First, the machine sleeping: the hold on sleep depends on the coordinator's session staying active, and one interrupted turn cost six and a half hours; a hold that does not depend on the session, or a power setting, is the owner's decision and is put to him. Second, the processor, once the lanes are back. Third, the old proofs without a saved wrong version, now about one in ten even among the newer ones. Two questions raised before the gap are with lanes that were cut off and are resumed: whether a scripted callee can write different words on each call within a trial (two lanes stopped on that belief), and how many verified rewrites convert a float to an integer with Rust's cast where the original's instruction behaves differently. Not accelerating: zero for eight hours against a baseline of 7,100 bytes an hour.
16:05The first 44 minutes after the standby, with the lane count taken from thirty to over a hundred on the owner's instruction to fill memory. Named functions rose by 728, to 36,817 of 37,413: the final naming pass, forty lanes of about 33 functions each with a brief that has each lane read every function in full, named in half an hour what a survey of strings and neighbours had failed on twice. Verified code rose by 6,168 bytes in 96 functions (8,400 bytes an hour, against 25,000 to 51,000 in last night's hours at thirty lanes); most lanes that ended in the window had sat through the standby and came back nearly empty, so the figure understates what a clean hour at this count would give, and the next hour is the measure. Two verified rewrites were withdrawn: an audit of float-to-integer conversions showed on the stock checker, with contracts widened to reach values that do not fit, that both differ from the original there (439 and 67 of 1,000 trials); their proofs of record drew only small floats. 288 more functions with such a conversion are being tested by script. One large function closed (4,490 bytes), the eighth by Haiku lanes: its lane had left it partly proven, and a fresh session found that nothing open was unwritten code. The shared evidence database is built (all 37,410 functions, rebuilt from the image in 90 seconds, a dossier per function in under a second) and is in the briefs. Memory is at the 2 GB reserve: the guard that stops a project process above 3 GB acted 14 times, all on naming lanes running the evidence collector the final-pass brief had pointed them to, and the floor guard has begun stopping lanes' link steps when available memory dips under the floor.Changed: the naming brief no longer points lanes at an earlier lane's collector, which takes 5 GB a run; it points at the shared database. Production, queue and Haiku briefs carry the database and the rule for conversions (brief version b26). Lane rules in the agent rules file gained eleven lessons from the large-function work, and the night's findings are in the devlog as entries of their own with fourteen lane entries, after the owner asked that findings be documented as they are made. One claim was held on the re-run because its lane had lost the rewrite file; five from another lane were returned to the pool because its library no longer held them. The three blockers. First, the processor: over a hundred lanes on 18 logical processors, with memory at the floor so that the floor guard now costs lanes their builds; the lane count is the owner's decision and the measured figures are put to him with a recommendation. Second, the conversion audit: 288 functions not yet tested, and the verified count may fall again. Third, the large functions still open after six and seven sessions. No lift ran in the window, for want of a lane and not for a blocker; a lift lane follows when naming ends. Accelerating against the 29-hour baseline (7,100 bytes an hour, which includes the eight idle hours); not against last night's hours.
18:05Two hours with the machine overloaded and then recovering, measured for what it cost. Between 16:02 and 18:00: verified code up by 38,121 bytes in 238 functions (19,400 bytes an hour), named functions up by 436 to 37,253 of 37,413, one withdrawal, no lift. The Luna lane count went from 115 at 15:55 to 30 at 17:50. At its worst, at 16:51 with 93 lanes, 181 threads were waiting for 18 logical processors: lanes' checker runs hit their time limits, the supervisor took fifteen minutes between imports, the regression runner needed 290 seconds a proof where it needs 13 on a free machine, and one command of the coordinator's did not start for 23 minutes. Luna lanes that ended in the two hours verified 281 functions and 33,842 bytes in 94 lane-hours, 359 bytes per lane-hour, against 1,000 to 2,300 in last night's hours at thirty lanes; most of what they did not finish is recorded as out of time or not reached. So the figure for more than a hundred lanes is now a clean one, and it is a third of what thirty lanes give. Naming is all but done: the final pass named 1,164 functions in two and a half hours, and one lane has the 160 that are left. The conversion audit withdrew a third rewrite and all three withdrawn today are proven again with corrected conversions and widened contracts; of 95 functions that needed the audit's test, 48 are tested. The audit also turned up something wider: on widened inputs, several verified rewrites differ from the original for reasons that are not the conversion. The first one examined is a clamp the original does with a signed comparison and the rewrite with an unsigned one.Changed in the window: starts were paused when memory reached the floor and the floor guard began stopping lanes' link steps; the coordinator's own supervising processes run above normal priority; and when the filler's window ended, with the owner asking whether more agents would help, it was restarted with a ceiling of thirty, which both of his options include, pending his answer. The re-run was corrected three times for the form in which lanes keep wrong versions: several contracts per function, paired contracts that share a name (the wrong one's verdict overwrote the right one's), and wrong versions built as a second library beside the output folder; 27 claims of two lanes held for that last reason are being re-run. The three blockers. First, the lane count, which is the owner's decision: every measurement now says thirty production lanes verify about three times what a hundred do. Second, rewrites that differ from the original outside the range their proofs drew: the conversion class is being closed, the signed and unsigned comparison is a second class, and an investigation lane is on four functions. Third, large functions: two are being worked state by state and route by route, and neither closed in the window. No lift ran, for want of a lane. Accelerating against the 31-hour baseline; below last night's hours.
19:05The first clean hour at thirty lanes since the overload, and the day's audit of proofs came to a head. Between 18:00 and 18:59: verified code up by 18,824 bytes in 291 functions net of six withdrawals (19,100 bytes an hour), three routines lifted, nothing named. Half the game's functions are now verified: 18,888 of 37,413. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 326 functions and 31,716 bytes in 67 lane-hours; most of those lanes had started during the overload. The audit that widens a proof's inputs has now tested every function it listed. It has withdrawn nine verified rewrites today: six whose float-to-integer conversion differs from the original out of range, one that clamps with the wrong signedness, one with a float comparison that differs when the operands are equal, and one whose cause is not yet located. Five are proven again, and each of the strengthening lanes found a second fault behind the first once it widened every input: a constant the original reads from the image, a second conversion, a branch the rewrite did not have. Eight more rewrites differ on widened inputs and are being reduced one by one before anything is done to them. Sixty passed the widened test without an extreme value reaching the code in question, which settles nothing. Naming has reached what can be read: of the 160 functions still unnamed, the final-pass lanes found them to be jumps into the part of the image that is encrypted on disk, entries that are not functions, and bare thunks. The pipeline on the public repository failed on the afternoon's last lift commit, for three reasons.Fixed in the hour. The pipeline's consistency check failed because five verified rewrites had files and no row in the index: three finishers and the coordinator had run the importer at once, and the last writer's copy of the index dropped the others' rows. The rows are restored and the importer and the withdrawal script now hold one lock from reading the index to writing it. The fault was on the safe side: verified work was not being counted. The second failure, the assembled library of all rewrites not building in one shard, is with a repair lane, and nothing further is integrated into the workspace crates until it reports; the third, formatting, is advisory. The coordinator's re-run was corrected twice more for the form of lanes' proofs (one library per group of functions; contract families under several claims), and 36 good claims held for those reasons were re-run and imported. A count in a changelog entry was wrong by the coordinator's own addition and was corrected. Naming lanes are no longer started for a function three lanes could not name. The three blockers. First, proofs with ordinary input ranges: nine rewrites withdrawn, eight under examination, sixty unsettled, and two classes (comparisons' signedness, float comparisons at equality) not yet searched for across the verified set; this is now the main trust item. Second, the pipeline. Third, the lane count, still the owner's decision and held at thirty. The 160 unnamed functions need either a capture of the encrypted code from the owner's own running copy or a decision on systematic names: both are his. Accelerating against the 32-hour baseline; level with the 16:00 to 18:00 window.
20:05An hour in which production held its rate and the audits kept finding things. Between 18:59 and 20:04: verified code up by 19,088 bytes in 53 functions net of seven removals (17,620 bytes an hour, against 8,559 over the last 33 hours), nothing lifted, five functions named. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 95 functions and 19,840 bytes in 20 lane-hours. The pipeline is green again: its assembler had been blaming compile errors on the wrong files, and with that corrected its manifest shows something larger, that 706 of 19,026 verified rewrites are left out of the assembled library because the published file does not build alone (helpers, constants and types that stayed in the proving lane's crate; in two cases the whole body). The two investigation lanes on widened inputs settled their eight functions: six are real differences and were withdrawn, each shown on the stock checker on trials the original completes, and two are cleared (an inconsistent widened contract; a failure only where the original itself faults). The causes add four classes to the morning's three: a float comparison's predicate at equality (now in two rewrites, with three more suspected from the instructions and not yet shown), call arguments in the wrong order, a float sum with unpinned operands, and a field read before the test that guards it. One rewrite proven again this morning was withdrawn a second time on a wider contract. One function withdrawn earlier was proven again, with a second fault found behind the first. Fifteen withdrawals of fourteen rewrites today; seven of the fourteen are back.Acted on in the hour. The assembler's correction, found by a repair lane, was reviewed and applied with three tests. The production brief is now version b27: six rules from the withdrawn rewrites with what a contract must reach to see each, and a rule that a lane builds its proving library from the files it publishes and nothing else. A tool lane is classifying the 706, writing a self-containment check for the importer, and proving repairs from the lanes' own source; they stay counted until it reports, with a devlog entry saying what the count includes. Three strengthening lanes have the withdrawn rewrites that have corrected copies, one of them charged with making the checker observe the three suspect comparisons before anything is withdrawn on a reading. The coordinator made two errors and corrected both: it imported one function by hand without its re-run (in the verified set for two minutes, taken out with a changelog entry), and its re-run was holding good claims for the way lanes store wrong versions, 36 of the hour's 39 held claims and 63 of the 83 held in all; the re-run now recognises four more layouts, requires the wrong version to be rejected by the same contract as the proof, and eleven lanes are being re-run. The three blockers. First, how much of the verified set differs from the original outside its proofs' ranges: every lane that widens inputs finds more, and no audit yet bounds it. Second, the 706 files that are not the code that was proven. Third, the coordinator's own re-run, corrected seven times today for the form of a lane's output: each correction was on the safe side, and each cost verified work an hour or more. Lifting had no lane this hour and gets one now. The lane count stays at thirty until the owner decides. Accelerating against the 33-hour baseline; level with the last three hours.
21:05The best hour for portable code so far, and two more ways found in which a proof can say less than it appears to. Between 20:04 and 20:59: verified code up by 20,549 bytes in 206 functions (22,417 bytes an hour, against 8,935 over the last 34 hours); 399 routines lifted, where the hour before had none. The lifts came from choosing lists by shape: every verified function of one small size that calls nothing. Two lanes took sixteen minutes each to show that 229 functions of 25 bytes are the ratio routine lifted five days ago and that 170 functions of 21 bytes are two small list and store routines; the coordinator ran all 456 differential tests itself before committing. 922 verified routines now have a portable counterpart. Of the sixteen rewrites withdrawn today for differences outside what their proofs covered, fourteen are proven again and counted, several with a second, third or fourth fault found behind the first once every input was widened. The first new gap: a contract of record that set two globals at addresses inside the code section, so that its proof never exercised the code it was about. With the addresses corrected the rewrite fails, as an audit had predicted from the original's instruction. 54 contracts of record place a value in code, 148 leave a write uncompared, and 288 share the signature. The second: by default the checker fills unused stack with a pattern, the manual lets a contract set the fill to zero, and 2,081 contracts of record do (11 per cent); three functions examined today passed only because of it, each reading a frame word it had not written. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 226 functions and 22,832 bytes in 44 lane-hours. An owner's request began in the hour: research into the Bevy engine as the platform under the finished game, in two lanes, one on Bevy's current state from primary sources and one on what this engine needs from a host.Acted on in the hour. The import now checks that every published file builds alone, with the tool lane's check wired into the finisher; an unattended prover has started on the 550 repaired files, each built alone and run against its lane's contract and wrong version before it may replace the published one. The lane that found the misplaced globals is correcting each such contract and running the verified rewrite through it, the 54 certain cases first, and will return a list to withdraw and a list to strengthen; its check for the driver will be adopted in a narrower form than it proposed (refuse code, gaps and addresses outside the image; warn for read-only data, where varying a constant is a wanted test). The production brief is now version b28: one stated layout for wrong-version contracts, how to turn an image address into the offset a contract wants and prove each value is seen, and a rule that the stack fill is not set to zero to make a proof pass. The coordinator's re-run was corrected for the eighth time today and now finds a wrong-version contract by its content in any folder of the lane; 22 claims held in the hour, 19 of them for that reason, are being run again. A fourth lift lane follows the third. The three blockers. First, proofs that cover less than they say: sixteen withdrawals on widened inputs, 54 to 288 contracts with misplaced or uncompared globals, 2,081 with a zero stack fill; each needs its own audit run and none is bounded yet. Second, the 706 published files that are not the proven code, now with a gate and a prover. Third, old proofs: the script that re-runs them confirms about nineteen an hour under this load, a third of what it tries, and its three workers go to the repaired-file prover when its current list ends. Stop doing: lift lanes on groups chosen by name. Accelerating against the 34-hour baseline; the highest verified rate at thirty lanes today.
22:05A steady hour of production, the day's withdrawals closed out, and a pipeline failure of the coordinator's own making. Between 20:59 and 22:04: verified code up by 18,039 bytes in 197 functions (16,651 bytes an hour, against 9,174 over the last 35 hours); 177 more routines lifted, to 1,099. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 216 functions and 16,782 bytes in 38 lane-hours. All sixteen rewrites withdrawn today for differing from the original outside what their proofs covered are proven again and counted, and the day's account is written up: none was caught by its contract of record, and at least eight had further faults behind the first. The lane on misplaced globals finished with no withdrawals: of 54 contracts that set a value inside the code section, 32 rewrites still pass once the contract is corrected, 5 have an original that faults on the corrected value, and 17 have no mechanical correction; of the 148 with an uncompared write, 45 were run and none fails. Its check is now in the driver: a contract that sets a value in code is refused. The first measurement of the zero stack fill, on 40 of 2,081 contracts: a third pass with the patterned fill as well; half fail only the comparison of calls, where the original hands a callee a buffer it has not yet filled; one in six fails on stored memory or globals, a real dependence on the zero. The unattended prover of repaired published files has settled 277 of 529: 82 hold with their wrong version rejected, 177 pass where the proving lane has no wrong version to run, 14 cannot run, and 4 fail, the two examined being an old vacuous contract and a repair that is not a pure renaming for one shape of script native. The largest function in hand had its ninth Haiku session and gained one stage.Acted on in the hour. The pipeline failed on two commits because the coordinator adopted the driver's placement check without moving the pinned hash of the reviewed driver that its own stock runner checks; the pin is corrected, the 296 script tests pass, and a change to the driver and its pin now go in one commit. Two more of the coordinator's slips were caught before they were committed or were corrected the same hour: a workspace-wide format run that reformatted four verified rewrites through a lift crate's path modules (restored; the modules are now marked so the formatter cannot follow them), and two figures run together in a changelog entry (corrected in an entry of its own). The integration script learned the path-module form and reviewed additions to the core crate. Lift lanes keep going on lists chosen by shape while they yield: five lanes gave 576 routines in the evening, with the yield falling as the functions get larger (229 and 170 of the two smallest sizes; 36 of 141 at 37 to 62 bytes). Stop doing, for tonight: the nine-session function. It has taken a Haiku lane for most of a day at one stage a session, its remaining blocks have each resisted a lane, and 197 other partly proven functions wait in the same queue; two lanes now take the next two of those, and the large one keeps its plan file for a later session with the stack map. The three blockers. First, proofs that cover less than they say, now with three measured audits and one of them closed without a withdrawal. Second, the 706 published files, with the prover two fifths through. Third, the coordinator's own process: three slips in an hour, each caught by a guard or a second look, none reaching a verified count. Accelerating against the 35-hour baseline; below the hour before, which had the re-imports.
23:05Production steady, the leaf functions lifted out, and two faults of the coordinator's own found in what it had changed during the evening. Between 22:04 and 23:02: verified code up by 14,859 bytes in 156 functions (15,371 bytes an hour, against 13,557 over the last 24 hours); 170 more routines lifted, to 1,269. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 192 functions and 18,408 bytes in 28 lane-hours, with one claim held. Nothing was withdrawn. Nine lanes on lists chosen by shape lifted 749 routines between 20:10 and 22:57; the last three showed the supply ending: a tenth of the functions of 26 to 36 bytes fell into families, and a harvest that matched all 1,977 remaining leaf functions against the lifted routines found 44. What remains is mostly one of a kind. The unattended prover finished the repaired published files: of 549 settled, 129 hold with their wrong version rejected, 371 pass their contract of record where the proving lane has no wrong version to run, 41 could not be run and 8 fail, the three examined being an old vacuous contract and a repair that is not a pure renaming for tail-jump script natives. Two partly proven functions were taken from the queue in place of the nine-session one: the first, of 973 bytes, was verified whole in one contract with four wrong versions; the second, of 2,781 bytes, gained six proven stages and stays open.Two faults of the coordinator's, both from the evening's own changes, found and corrected. First, the paragraphs added to the production brief as versions b27 and b28 were inserted into the brief makers with their backslashes unescaped, so that in every brief generated from 20:00 three paths lost a letter to a control character (the contracts folder, the verdicts folder, the rewrites folder). Luna lanes inferred the right names and their imports went through; one Haiku lane followed the text literally and wrote its contracts under a mangled name. The makers are repaired on validated copies and a freshly generated brief was checked; the fault was found by reading a lane's report, not by any guard, and the makers' output is now checked for control characters. Second, the adoption of the driver's placement check broke the pipeline twice (the unmoved pin of the driver's hash, then two packages the module imported at load); both are fixed and the pipeline has a green run since. The coordinator's re-run gained a fallback for a lane whose wrong-version library does not export the right version, which had blocked a lane of 13; and it showed its own limit: at 300 trials it missed a wrong version that fails on 6 trials in 1,200, held a good claim, and passed it at the contract's own count. Next: the 500 repaired files that pass go into the verified tree as one reviewed change, each checked to build alone; the stack-fill audit runs through the night; lifting moves to classes, where 117 with four or more verified methods and none lifted hold about 105,000 verified bytes, and two such lanes have started. The three blockers. First, proofs that cover less than they say: the zero stack fill (2,081 contracts, audit running), uncompared writes (103 of 148 not yet run), old proofs with no wrong version (371 in the prover's sample of the unbuildable files alone). Second, the coordinator's process under its own pace of change: five slips in two hours, each small, two reaching lanes. Changes to the brief makers and to the checker folder are now made on a copy, validated, and only then put in place. Third, the lane count, still the owner's decision and held at thirty; and the host platform questions put to him. Accelerating against the 24-hour baseline, slightly.

entry.title: Haiku lanes on three large functions that earlier lanes left partly proven
entry.summary: Three lanes run by Claude Haiku 5.5 each took one function of 2,200 to 2,900 bytes that three or four lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. One closed its function in 36 minutes; two moved theirs further and stopped. None of the three is counted as verified today: the one proof that closed is held back because of the form of its rewrite. Each lane also found something the earlier lanes had got wrong.
entry.content:
Three lanes run by Claude Haiku 5.5 each took one function of 2,200 to 2,900 bytes that three or four lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. One closed its function in 36 minutes; two moved theirs further and stopped. None of the three is counted as verified today: the one proof that closed is held back because of the form of its rewrite. Each lane also found something the earlier lanes had got wrong.

What was asked

The owner asked for Haiku lanes on the harder work where the other model's lanes are struggling. The first test was the queue of functions partly proven in stages, which holds the most deferred code: 72 functions, 186,000 bytes.

What was found

Lane's functionResultTime used of 95 minutesWhat it found
A renderer set-up routine, 2,491 bytes, 60 call sitesOne rewrite passes six contracts at 1,000 trials each; every wrong version fails. The coordinator re-ran all six: they reproduce.36The earlier deferral was wrong. It said the main path needs a capture from the running game because a callee lies in the part of the program that is encrypted on disk. A call site can be replaced by a scripted stand-in whether or not its target is encrypted: with all 52 direct call sites replaced and one function-table slot planted, the original completes every trial.
A proximity sweep, 2,215 bytesPartly proven, further than before: two new stages at 1,000 trials, four earlier ones replayed. The loop, the visited-set check and one flag branch remain.31An earlier stage's claim was wrong. Its contract gave a callee an answer sequence to alternate between two answers, but a sequence is consumed per call within a trial, and this callee is called once per trial, so only the first answer was ever given and one of the two paths never ran. The manual describes the sequence this way; the earlier contract misused it.
An audio occlusion update, 2,924 bytesPartly proven: six earlier stages replayed and one new mixed stage, each at 1,000 trials. Two things block the whole function.22Two gaps in the earlier stages. On the early-exit path the original returns whatever was already in the return register and the rewrite returns zero; the stage that "passed" did not compare that register. And two paths store a stack word the function has not written; the rewrite assumes zero, and the stages fail when the stack is filled with anything else.

Verified The six contracts of the first function were re-run by the coordinator on the stock checker against the lane's library: 6,000 trials pass and each wrong version is rejected.

Verified The answer-sequence behaviour is as the driver's manual states it. Whether other accepted proofs used a sequence for a callee that is called once per trial has not been counted yet.

Inferred The unwritten stack word in the third function is probably filled by a callee through a pointer argument: the lane's contracts leave the callees' writes through pointers unmodelled. The lane did not test this.

What was decided or recommended

  • The first function's rewrite is not imported. Its proof holds, but the rewrite keeps the original's stack as an array and mirrors every push into it. That carries the original's instruction sequence over instead of writing the behaviour as Rust, and the project's first rule allows only the second in the repository; a doubtful case stays out. It is recorded as held, with the reason, and needs rewriting in the project's form and proving again on the same six contracts. The lane very likely chose this form to reproduce stale stack words exactly, which is the same problem that stopped the third lane.
  • Two lanes stopped with most of their time unused while a named next step remained: read the callers to see whether the return value is used; model the callee's write through its pointer argument; continue to the loop. The launch note for these lanes gets a rule against stopping early, and a rule about the form of a large rewrite, before any more are started.
  • A count of accepted proofs that use an answer sequence for a callee called once per trial goes on the list of open trust work.
  • A deferral that says a function needs a capture from the running game because a callee is encrypted is to be re-read: 38 functions are in that queue.

How to reproduce it

Each lane's folder holds its stage contracts, the rewrite and its wrong versions, and a note for the next lane. The coordinator's re-run takes the contracts unchanged and runs them with the repository's driver.

What was confusing or went wrong

The work was paused by the owner after this batch, so the two unfinished functions were not sent back to their lanes. Lanes were not told what form a large rewrite must have beyond the standard for small ones, and the one lane that finished solved a hard problem in a form that cannot be published.

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 10 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. These rows are the Claude coordinator's; a second coordinator session runs lanes of another model on the same repository and keeps its own reviews. The last rows before these are in "Hourly reviews, 6 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour: whether the work is still pointed at the goal, what the last hour produced, what weakened confidence in the results, and what changes because of it. One row is added here per review. These rows are the Claude coordinator's; a second coordinator session runs lanes of another model on the same repository and keeps its own reviews. The last rows before these are in "Hourly reviews, 6 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
11:10Work resumed today with a different lane model on this side: Claude Haiku 5.5 subagents, by the owner's instruction, first as a trial and then for the harder functions the other session's lanes are not getting through. 16,958 functions are verified, 45.3% of the functions. Throughput: one Haiku lane on 20 small functions verified 19 in 30 minutes (910 bytes, about 1,800 bytes per lane-hour, limited by the size of its batch), level with the earlier model's record per function; the entry "A smaller model on the production brief" has the comparison. Trust: the coordinator re-ran all 19 proofs on the stock checker before importing them, and all hold with their wrong versions rejected. One of the 19 is narrower than it looks (a store into the function's own argument slot is invisible to the checker) and says so in its result. Direction: three Haiku lanes are now on large functions that three or four lanes of the other model each left partly proven; the queue of such functions holds 186,000 bytes in 72 functions, the largest queue of deferred work. From their logs after five minutes, all three had read the earlier stage material and one had a combined stage contract passing 1,000 trials with its wrong version caught. The largest risk nothing runs against: two coordinators commit to one working tree with no lock between them, and the pipeline on the public repository has failed on every run since 8 October (a script test that loads the wrong module, and a lift test that includes a rewrite withdrawn on 7 October). Workstation: 13 GB of 47.6 free, no paging, nothing left behind; the registry shows 15 lanes of the other session and 3 of this one, which is at or just over the owner's limit of 15 depending on whether the other session's dispatcher and monitor are counted.Changed in the hour: a lane-by-name import (a broad pass would take rows the other session is holding for review); a re-run of a new model's claims before import; a launch note for Haiku lanes (a log line every five minutes, one checker worker and one build at a time, since the machine is shared); the queue brief builder can make a lane for chosen functions under its own lane series; the dashboard shows Claude subagent lanes with their model and prompt. The importer now keeps the indentation it finds in the verified index, after its first commit today rewrote the whole file in a different one (content checked identical). Stop doing: the re-run at the full trial count as a gate for small-function lanes; it took 17 minutes for a 30-minute lane, and 300 trials with the wrong version is enough to catch a claim that does not reproduce. No more Haiku lanes are started while the registry is at the limit. The pipeline failures are flagged to the owner as their own piece of work.
22:10Work started again at 20:30 at the owner's word, with a mix he asked for: Luna lanes for the bulk and Claude Haiku lanes for the harder functions, and 8 GB of memory kept available for his own use. Ten lanes were running by 20:48: seven Luna (four on small functions, one on larger ones, one re-running 350 proofs made on early checker versions, one on deferred functions that pass doubles in vector registers) and three Haiku (the two large functions left partly proven in the morning, and a rewrite of the held function in the project's form). Then the laptop went to sleep at about 20:57 and woke at 22:06. Every lane stood still for 70 minutes; the three Haiku lanes lost their connection and ended, and one push failed. Throughput for the hour is therefore close to nothing: 16,958 verified, unchanged, with 9 functions recorded as verified in lanes that are still running and not yet imported. Trust: nothing new was imported, so nothing to weigh; the Luna lanes run on the plain production brief for the first time from this coordinator, and their claims will be re-run before import as the first Haiku lane's were. One early sign from the Haiku lanes after they were resumed: the lane on the audio function found that the only caller discards the return value that stopped the morning's lane, which is the check the new launch note tells lanes to make. Workstation: 15.8 GB available of 47.6, no paging, both guards alive.Changed in the hour. The laptop is asked to stay awake while the session works, and the watch never waits more than four minutes, since the hold lapses after about five idle ones; a closed lid still stops everything, and the owner knows. The three Haiku lanes were resumed from their own state with a new time limit. A launcher for Luna lanes as plain Codex processes replaces the Muse launcher for now, with the same restart rule. A floor guard keeps 8 GB available: no lane is started under 10 GB, and if available memory stays under 8 GB for half a minute the project's largest build is stopped. Launch note h2 for Haiku lanes: do not stop while time and a next step remain; write the behaviour as Rust and never mirror the original's stack; a stack word read before it is written usually comes from a callee's pointer argument; check whether any caller reads a return value before deferring over it. The dashboard and the status script count Luna processes. Stale rows of the morning's other session, 26 still marked as running, are marked stopped when their lane has been silent for an hour. Stop doing: nothing dropped this hour. The Luna lanes' time limits ran through the sleep, so most will stop short of their batches; what they did not reach goes back to the pool. Held at ten lanes until the first Luna claims pass the re-run.
23:05The first full hour of the evening's mix. 16,992 functions verified, 45.4% of the functions and 32.6% of the code by size: 35 more than at the last review, after one withdrawal. Twelve lanes ran, eight Luna and four Haiku. Throughput by lane kind, in the lanes' real working time (three of the first Luna lanes lost 70 minutes to the laptop's sleep, so their own clocks say less than they did). Luna on small functions: 43 verified in seven lanes that have ended or are well along; the uninterrupted ones are making 10 to 27 functions per lane-hour, against 29 to 38 in the earlier model's record and 37 in this morning's one Haiku lane. Luna on larger functions: 1 of 5, with 4 deferred. Luna on the queue of deferred functions that pass doubles: 4 verified in two lanes, 1 deferred. Luna re-running old proofs: 291 of 312 run hold on the current checker in the first lane, 522 of 522 so far in the two that are running. Haiku on large functions left partly proven: two closed and imported (2,924 and 2,491 bytes, the second being the function held in the morning, now written in the project's form), four more in progress. Trust: every claim was re-run by the coordinator's scripts before import, 40 of 40 from Luna and 2 of 2 from Haiku holding. The re-run itself failed twice in the hour, both times by running a lane's contracts against the wrong library, and the second time it marked nine good claims as not holding before the fault was seen; nothing was imported or withdrawn on it. One function was withdrawn: its old proof is vacuous on the current checker. Twenty old proofs could not be run at all and stay counted as an open item, fourteen of them because their contracts give a stack argument in a form the current driver refuses, which may mean they were made on a private copy of the driver. Direction: the Haiku lanes keep finding errors in earlier stage work (a stage that read two helpers' answers from the wrong register and so always saw zero; sixteen replayed stages that never reach the part of the function they were taken to cover; a second deferral for an encrypted callee that was no blocker). The largest risk nothing runs against is unchanged: the pipeline on the public repository has failed since 8 October. Workstation: 16.4 GB available of 47.6, no paging, processor at 100% for much of the hour.Changed in the hour. A supervisor for the Luna side finishes each lane when it ends (re-run, hold, import by lane name, publish) and keeps eight running while 10 GB or more is available. The re-run finds a lane's library whether the contract names it or the lane passed it through the environment, handles a function proven by several stage contracts, and reports a run in which every trial fails with no failed comparison as its own fault, which can no longer hold a claim. The importer commits the index when only the recorded checker version changed. All four Haiku lanes on large functions stopped between minute 18 and minute 37 of 95 with their next step named in their own reports, despite the launch note's rule; each was sent back in with its context and the steps in order, and the note now says the limit is a deadline to compute and check, and that an early report with work open is sent back. Stop doing: taking a Haiku lane's first report on a large function as its result. Held at twelve lanes although the owner's limit is fifteen: the limit exists for heat and the processor is already at its ceiling. Open and recorded: the fourteen unrunnable contracts, three tracked rewrites that do not compile, three missing contracts, and a count of accepted proofs that script a once-per-trial callee with an answer sequence.

The coordinator then re-ran all 19 proofs itself on the stock checker: all 19 hold and every deliberately wrong version is rejected. On small functions it is level with the lanes the process was tuned on. Nothing is measured yet for large functions.

What was asked

The owner asked for Haiku subagents to be tried in place of the earlier lane model, starting with one lane, and for a judgement of whether it is better or worse. The earlier model could not be run alongside, so the comparison is against its recorded lanes of the same kind: small-function production lanes on checker versions 6 to 8.

What was found

Verified The figures for the Haiku lane are from its results file, its log and the coordinator's re-run. The earlier model's are computed from its lanes' results files and launcher logs.

Verified The lane reported a limit of the checker that no lane of the earlier model had reported: a function that stores into the stack slot of its own last argument is not seen doing so, because the worker's return path overwrites that word before the comparison. The lane read the worker's source to confirm it, kept the one affected function as verified and listed the gap in that function's result. Another session's notes from 8 October describe the same limit, so the finding is independent, not new. An argument slot belongs to the called function, so a store there is not behaviour its caller can observe; the proof is narrower than it looks and says so.

Unknown Whether this holds for large functions. One lane of 20 small functions is a thin sample, and most of the code still to verify is in functions of 1,000 bytes and more.

What was decided or recommended

  • The 19 rewrites were imported after the re-run, by lane name.
  • Three Haiku lanes were started on large functions that several lanes of another model had left partly proven in stages. That is where the owner wants Haiku used, and it is the measurement that is missing.
  • A lane of a model with no record here has its claims re-run by the coordinator before import. For small functions the re-run is cut from the full trial count to 300 trials: at the full count it took 17 minutes for a lane that itself took 30.
  • The note given to a Haiku lane at launch now asks for a log line at least every five minutes. The first lane wrote five lines in half an hour, and the coordinator's five-minute report had nothing to show.

How to reproduce it

The baseline is every small-function production lane with a checker version 6, 7 or 8 marker: batch size from its list, verified rows from its results file, minutes from the launcher's lines in its log. The re-run takes each contract the lane wrote, unchanged, and runs it with the repository's driver against the library the contract names; the driver runs the declared wrong version with it.

What was confusing or went wrong

The brief is given whole to a lane of the earlier model. A subagent reads it from a file, and its file reader cuts lines after about 2,000 characters; the brief has longer ones. The lane was given a copy with line breaks added at sentence ends and nothing else changed. The lane also wrote its report under a different file name than the brief asks for, because of a rule of its own environment about that file type; the launch note now says the brief's name is allowed in its scratch folder.
